m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Check your computer's RAM, chip, and virtualization support against Android Studio's real requirements.
  • Install Android Studio and finish the setup wizard on your operating system.
  • Decide whether you'll test apps on the emulator or on your own Android phone.
  • Install a JDK so you can run the plain-Java programs in Week 2.

On the first day of an Android class, someone always opens Android Studio for the first time and watches a progress bar labeled "Downloading components" for the next 30 minutes. The installer is around 1 GB, and the setup wizard then pulls several more gigabytes: the Android SDK, build tools, and a full Android system image for the emulator.

Do all of it at home, on good Wi-Fi, before Week 1. Then class time goes to building apps.

#What you're installing

Android Studio is Google's free tool for making Android apps. It's really four tools in one window:

  • The editor, where you write Java and design screens in XML.
  • The Android SDK, the libraries and build tools every app is compiled against.
  • Gradle, the build system that turns your code into an installable app file (an APK).
  • The emulator, a virtual Android phone that runs in a window on your computer.

The emulator is the hungry one. Android Studio alone is comfortable on 8 GB of RAM; running a virtual phone next to it is where 16 GB starts to matter.

#Check your computer first

These are Google's published minimums:

Windows macOS Linux
OS 64-bit Windows 10 or newer macOS 12 or newer 64-bit distro with GNOME, KDE, or Unity; glibc 2.31+
RAM 8 GB for Studio; 16 GB to also run the emulator same same
Free disk 8 GB; 16 GB with the emulator (an SSD helps a lot) same same
CPU 64-bit Intel or AMD from about 2017 on, with virtualization (VT-x or AMD-V) enabled Apple M-series, or 6th-gen Intel Core or newer same as Windows
Screen 1280 x 800 same same

Windows and Linux PCs with ARM processors (some thin laptops, such as Snapdragon models) aren't supported yet. On a Chromebook, Android Studio runs inside ChromeOS's Linux environment, and it can only send apps to a real phone plugged in over USB, not to an emulator.

Here's how to find your numbers:

  • Windows: press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager, click Performance, then Memory for RAM. Click CPU and look for Virtualization: Enabled.
  • macOS: Apple menu > About This Mac. It shows the chip (Apple M1, M2, and so on, or Intel) and the memory.
  • Linux: run these in a terminal.

Read the total column of the Mem: row for RAM. The second command counts CPU cores that support hardware virtualization: any number above 0 is good news, and 0 means it's missing or switched off in your BIOS.

💡 Tip

Only 8 GB of RAM? You can still take this class. A real Android phone over USB costs your computer almost nothing, while an emulator can take 2 to 4 GB of RAM on its own. Any phone from the last several years works.

#Download and install

Download from the official page at developer.android.com/studio (linked at the bottom). Accept the license, then pick the file for your system.

Windows

  1. Download the Windows .exe installer.
  2. Double-click it. On the components screen, leave Android Virtual Device ticked; that's the emulator.
  3. Accept the default install folder, click through to Finish, and let it launch Android Studio.

If Windows asks whether to allow the app to make changes, click Yes.

macOS

  1. Check About This Mac first. Download Mac with Apple chip for M1 and newer, or Mac with Intel chip for Intel Macs. The wrong one either won't open or runs painfully slowly.
  2. Open the .dmg and drag Android Studio into Applications.
  3. Open it from Applications. When macOS warns that it was downloaded from the internet, click Open.

Google is phasing out support for Intel Macs, so on an older Intel Mac expect the emulator to be slow and lean on a real phone instead.

Linux

Download the .tar.gz, unpack it into /opt, and start it from the bin folder (adjust the file name to match your download):

On 64-bit Ubuntu, Google also asks for a few 32-bit libraries:

Once Android Studio is open, choose Tools > Create Desktop Entry so it appears in your app menu.

Chromebook

  1. Turn on Linux: open Settings, search for Linux development environment, and click Set up. Give it at least 15 GB of disk if it asks.
  2. Download the ChromeOS .deb file.
  3. In the Files app, move the .deb from Downloads into Linux files.
  4. Open the Terminal app and install it (the exact file name will differ):
  1. Launch Android Studio from the Launcher, or run /opt/android-studio/bin/studio in the terminal.

Remember that on ChromeOS you'll run apps on a phone plugged in over USB, so have one and a data cable ready.

#Run the setup wizard

The first launch opens a setup wizard. These choices work for this class:

  1. Import settings: choose not to import (unless you've used Android Studio before).
  2. Install type: Standard. It picks the SDK, the emulator, and a recent Android version for you.
  3. Theme: your choice.
  4. License agreements: this is where people get stuck. The left side lists several licenses; click each one and select Accept. The Finish button stays grey until every license is accepted.
  5. Click Finish and wait. On slow Wi-Fi the downloads can take 20 minutes or more.

You know it worked when you land on the Welcome to Android Studio window, with New Project, Open, and More Actions.

The wizard puts the SDK in one of these folders. Make a note of yours, because several fixes later in the course need it:

OS Default SDK location
Windows C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Android\Sdk
macOS ~/Library/Android/sdk
Linux and Chromebook ~/Android/Sdk

#When the install goes wrong

These are the four problems that actually come up, and their fixes.

The wizard's Finish button won't light up. A license is still unaccepted. Click every license name in the left list, one at a time, and select Accept for each.

Strange build errors that mention your SDK folder. Some build tools break on paths with spaces or non-English letters, such as a Windows user name like Zoë Kim. Create a simple folder like C:\Android\Sdk and choose it as the SDK location in the wizard. If you already installed, change it in Settings > Languages & Frameworks > Android SDK.

The download stalls or fails halfway. School and library networks sometimes block the SDK servers. Try home Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot, then restart Android Studio; the wizard picks up the missing parts.

The emulator complains about hardware acceleration. Virtualization is off in your computer's firmware. The next two lessons cover the fix, and a phone over USB sidesteps the problem entirely.

#One more tool for Week 2: a JDK

Android Studio carries its own Java for building apps. In Week 2, though, you'll run small plain-Java programs from a terminal, and that needs a separate JDK (Java Development Kit).

Install Eclipse Temurin from adoptium.net, version 21 or newer (the LTS version the site offers by default is fine). On Windows, the installer has an option called Set JAVA_HOME variable; switch it on, and leave Add to PATH on. Then open a new terminal and check:

Both should print a version number of 21 or higher. If you get command not found or 'java' is not recognized, close the terminal and open a fresh one, since terminals only read the PATH when they start. If that doesn't help on Windows, rerun the installer and make sure both options are on.

  • Download Android Studio (opens in a new tab): the download page, with every OS's file.
  • Configure hardware acceleration for the Android Emulator (opens in a new tab): what to switch on if the emulator is slow or refuses to start.

What you'll learn

  • Create a Java project from the Empty Views Activity template, not the Compose one.
  • Set up an emulator or connect your own phone with USB debugging.
  • Run the app, change it, and run it again.
  • Confirm your JDK runs a plain-Java program from the terminal.

An installed IDE proves nothing until it builds something. The test for this lesson is simple: a phone screen, real or virtual, that says Hello from and then your name. Getting there touches every part of the setup at once: the project template, the Gradle build, the device, and the install. If any piece is broken, you'll find out now instead of in the middle of Week 1.

#Create the project

  1. On the Welcome window, click New Project. (If a project is already open, use File > New > New Project.)
  2. Under Phone and Tablet, choose Empty Views Activity and click Next.
  3. Fill in the form:
    • Name: HelloC4T
    • Package name: com.example.helloc4t (filled in for you)
    • Save location: the default AndroidStudioProjects folder
    • Language: Java
    • Minimum SDK: API 24 ("Nougat"; Android 7.0)
    • Build configuration language: Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts), the default
  4. Click Finish.

⚠️ Watch out

The template named just Empty Activity sits right next to Empty Views Activity, and it builds screens with Jetpack Compose in Kotlin. If your form has no Language dropdown, you picked that one. Click Previous and choose Empty Views Activity.

Your build files will be written in Kotlin DSL even though your app is Java. That's normal: the build configuration language and the app's language are two separate choices, and you'll only open the build files now and then.

Now Android Studio runs its first Gradle sync, downloading the libraries the template needs. Watch the progress bar at the bottom right. The first sync on a fresh install can take several minutes, and clicking around while it runs only slows it down.

#Look at what you got

Open app > java > com.example.helloc4t > MainActivity.java. The template wrote this for you:

Only one line matters today: setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) tells Android which screen layout to show. The rest pads the screen so your content doesn't hide under the status bar. Week 1 takes it apart line by line.

Then open app > res > layout > activity_main.xml. If it shows a picture of a phone, click Code (or Split) at the top right of the editor:

This is the whole screen: a layout that fills the display, holding one piece of text pinned to all four edges, which centers it.

#Give it somewhere to run

Pick one of these. If you have both, set up both; a phone is faster, and the emulator is handy when your phone is across the room.

Emulator

  1. Open Device Manager from the right-hand toolbar, or View > Tool Windows > Device Manager. The Standard setup sometimes creates a device for you (often named something like Medium Phone). If one is listed, skip to step 6.
  2. Click +, then Create Virtual Device.
  3. Pick a recent Pixel phone profile and click Next.
  4. Choose a system image with a recent API level and let it download. An Apple-silicon Mac needs an arm64 image; Intel and AMD computers need x86_64. Android Studio normally shows the right kind first.
  5. Click Finish.
  6. Click the play button next to the device. The first boot is slow, often a minute or two.

Your Android phone

  1. On the phone, open Settings > About phone and tap Build number seven times, until it says you're now a developer. (On some brands, Build number is under Software information.)
  2. Go back to Settings, open System > Developer options, and turn on USB debugging.
  3. Plug the phone into your computer with a cable that carries data. Many cheap cables only charge.
  4. Unlock your phone. When it asks Allow USB debugging?, tick Always allow from this computer and tap Allow.

On Windows, a few phone brands also need the maker's USB driver before they appear; the OEM USB drivers page below lists them. The phone shows up in Android Studio's device dropdown by its model name.

#Run it

Pick your emulator or phone in the device dropdown on the toolbar, then click the green Run triangle (Shift + F10 on Windows and Linux, Control + R on macOS).

The first build is the slowest you'll ever see; later ones reuse most of the work. On an emulator, the screen appears in Android Studio's Running Devices panel. You should see a white screen with Hello World! in the middle.

#Prove you control it

Right now you're looking at the template, not your work. In activity_main.xml, change the text line:

Use your own name, then click Run again. A few seconds later the screen shows your message. Press the device's home button and look in the app drawer: there's your app, with the green Android icon and the label HelloC4T.

#Prove your JDK works too

Week 2 runs plain Java programs outside Android Studio. Make a file named Hello.java anywhere outside your Android project, such as on your Desktop:

In a terminal in that folder, compile it and run it:

You should see the same two lines as the output above, with your own Java version on the second line. (Java 11 and newer also accept the shortcut java Hello.java, which compiles and runs in one step.) If both the app and this program run, your setup is done.

#If it didn't work

The Run button is grey, or the dropdown says No Devices. The emulator hasn't finished booting, or the phone isn't authorized. Wait for the emulator's home screen, or unlock your phone, unplug it, plug it back in, and look for the Allow USB debugging? prompt.

There's no Language option when creating the project. You picked Empty Activity. Go back and choose Empty Views Activity.

The phone charges but never appears. Try another cable first; it's the cause more often than anything else. Then try a different USB port, and make sure USB debugging is still on.

The Gradle sync never finishes. Leave it for ten minutes on a first install. If it fails with a red message, use File > Sync Project with Gradle Files to retry, and see the next lesson's Gradle section.

#Further reading

  • Create and manage virtual devices (opens in a new tab): every Device Manager option, including how to edit a device's RAM.
  • Run apps on a hardware device (opens in a new tab): developer options, USB debugging, and wireless debugging over Wi-Fi.
  • Install OEM USB drivers (opens in a new tab): the list of phone makers' Windows drivers.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Know what happens in each 90-minute class and which pages to use if you miss one.
  • Name, save, and share your projects so you can find old work later.
  • Ask for help with the details an instructor needs to answer in seconds.
  • Fix a failed Gradle sync, a slow or broken emulator, and a computer that runs out of memory.

Most first-week trouble in Android comes from one of three places: Gradle can't finish syncing, the emulator can't get hardware acceleration, or the computer runs out of memory. Each has a short list of fixes, and they're all below. First, how the class itself works, because knowing the rhythm makes it easier to keep up.

#What a class session looks like

The class meets live online once a week for 1.5 hours, for six weeks. A session usually goes like this:

  1. Review and questions (10 minutes). Last week's ideas, plus anything that broke while you practiced.
  2. New ideas (25 minutes). The week's concepts, explained with code on screen.
  3. Code-along (40 minutes). You build a small app alongside the instructor, one step at a time.
  4. Practice (15 minutes). You start the week's exercises with help on hand.

Each week on this site has three matching pages: Notes (the concepts), Code-along (the app you build), and Practice (exercises with hints and solutions you can reveal). If you miss a class, those three pages cover everything that happened.

Three habits that keep class time for coding:

  • Open Android Studio and start your emulator five minutes early. A cold emulator can take two minutes to boot, and nobody wants to wait for that live.
  • Mute unless you're talking, and unmute when you're stuck. Saying "my build failed" out loud is how a whole class learns the fix.
  • Share your screen with the error showing. A red error message usually tells the instructor exactly what's wrong in seconds.

#Keep your projects where you can find them

Android Studio saves as you type, so there's no Save button to forget. What matters is where projects live and what they're called.

  • Keep every project in the default AndroidStudioProjects folder in your home folder.
  • Make a new project for each week's code-along, named so you'll recognize it in a month: Week1Hello, Week3BusinessCard, and so on. One project reused for everything makes it impossible to look back at earlier work.
  • To send a project to an instructor or move it to another computer, use File > Export > Export to Zip File. It leaves out the big build folders, which Gradle recreates anyway.
  • To reopen a project, use File > Open and select the project's top folder, the one containing settings.gradle.kts, not the app folder inside it.

💡 Tip

If you already know Git, turn on version control for each project and commit at the end of every class. The template already includes a sensible .gitignore, so build output stays out of your history.

#How to ask for help and get a fast answer

"It doesn't work" can mean a hundred things. A good help request has three parts:

  1. What you did: "I pressed Run with the emulator selected."
  2. What happened, word for word: the first red line in the Build window, copied or screenshotted, not a summary of it.
  3. What you already tried: "I synced again and restarted Android Studio."

The first error matters most. One mistake often causes a cascade of later errors that disappear once the first one is fixed, so scroll up and click the top red line in the Build window before you read anything else.

#Find your problem

#Problem 1: Gradle sync fails

Symptoms: a banner saying Gradle sync failed, red messages in the Build window, or red underlines under every import androidx... line.

Work through these in order and stop when it's fixed:

  1. Check your connection. The first sync downloads libraries, and school or library networks sometimes block those downloads. Try home Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot.
  2. Sync again. Use File > Sync Project with Gradle Files. A sync that was interrupted halfway often succeeds on the second try.
  3. Check the Gradle JDK. Open Settings (Android Studio > Settings on macOS) and go to Build, Execution, Deployment > Build Tools > Gradle. Set Gradle JDK to the bundled JetBrains Runtime, usually labeled jbr-21. A missing or wrong JDK here causes errors such as Unsupported class file major version.
  4. Clear caches. File > Invalidate Caches, tick the options, then Invalidate and Restart.
  5. Read the first error, not the last. In the Build window, click the top red line. The real cause is almost always there.

#Problem 2: the emulator is slow or won't start

The emulator needs your CPU's virtualization features. Without them it either refuses to start or crawls.

Windows

  1. Restart into your BIOS or UEFI settings (usually F2, F10, F12, or Del while the computer boots; it varies by brand) and enable Intel Virtualization Technology (VT-x) or AMD SVM.
  2. Back in Windows, open the Start menu, search for Turn Windows features on or off, tick Windows Hypervisor Platform, click OK, and restart.
  3. Task Manager's Performance > CPU page should now say Virtualization: Enabled.

macOS

Apple-silicon and recent Intel Macs have acceleration built in. If an emulator won't boot on an Apple chip, check that its system image is arm64: in Device Manager, open the device's menu and look at its details. Delete any x86_64 device and create a new one.

Linux

The emulator uses KVM. On Ubuntu, install it and add yourself to the kvm group, then log out and back in:

Chromebook

ChromeOS can't run the Android Emulator from Android Studio. Run your apps on a phone over USB instead; it's faster anyway.

The emulator can check acceleration for you. Run it from the SDK's emulator folder, using your own SDK location from the install lesson (this is the Linux default):

When everything is right, the output includes a line saying that WHPX (Windows), Hypervisor.Framework (macOS), or KVM (Linux) is installed and usable.

#Problem 3: not enough memory

If your computer freezes, or the emulator closes itself during a build, you're out of RAM.

  • Close browser tabs, games, and video apps you don't need. A browser with many tabs can use several gigabytes on its own.
  • Give the emulator less memory: in Device Manager, edit the device, open the advanced settings, and set RAM to 2 GB.
  • Turn on File > Power Save Mode while you're reading rather than typing; it pauses background code analysis.
  • Best of all, run on your phone and close the emulator entirely.

#Check devices with adb

When Android Studio insists there's no device, adb (Android Debug Bridge, in the SDK's platform-tools folder) gives a straight answer. Run the line for your system in a terminal:

Windows

macOS

Linux and Chromebook

A healthy result lists each device with the word device after it:

If a phone shows unauthorized, unlock it and accept the Allow USB debugging? prompt. If nothing is listed at all, swap the cable or the USB port, since a charge-only cable is the usual cause.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't fix a broken setup by downloading SDK folders or Gradle files from forums or video descriptions. Almost every problem above is solved inside Android Studio's own settings, and copied files usually bring new errors with them.

#Further reading

  • Troubleshoot known issues with Android Studio (opens in a new tab): Google's list of current bugs and their workarounds.
  • Android Debug Bridge (adb) (opens in a new tab): everything adb can do beyond listing devices.
  • Troubleshoot the Android Emulator (opens in a new tab): fixes for an emulator that won't boot, stays black, or runs slowly.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find your way around the Android view of a project: java, res, manifests, and Gradle Scripts.
  • Explain what each line of the template's MainActivity.java does, and why there's no main().
  • Read the manifest and the app's build.gradle.kts well enough to change the app's name, version, and minimum Android version.
  • Describe the steps between clicking Run and seeing your app on screen.

Open a brand-new project and the Project panel already shows folders called manifests, java, res, and Gradle Scripts, plus a file named libs.versions.toml that looks like a typo. It's a lot. The good news: you'll edit about three of these files every week, a few now and then, and the rest almost never. Knowing which is which is most of what makes Android Studio feel manageable.

#The Android view sorts files by job

The Project panel on the left has a dropdown at the top. Keep it on Android. That view groups files by what they do rather than how they sit on disk:

Four areas, four jobs. java holds your code. res (short for resources) holds everything that isn't code: layouts, text, colors, images. manifests describes the app to the Android system. Gradle Scripts say how to build it all. The two (test) folders are for automated tests, which this course doesn't use.

#MainActivity.java: code that Android calls

An Activity is one screen of an app plus the Java code behind it. Here's the template's activity again, with a comment on every important line:

Look for main() and you won't find one. In a console program, your code starts at the top and runs to the bottom. In an Android app, Android creates your Activity object and calls its methods when things happen: the screen opens, the user leaves, the phone rotates. Your job is to fill in those methods. onCreate() is the first one called, which is why setup code goes there.

Resumed is the state you see as "the app is open". Press Home and the activity slides to Stopped; come back and it climbs to Resumed again.

Every androidx... import comes from AndroidX, Google's current support libraries. If an online tutorial imports android.support.v7..., it predates 2018 and won't compile in a new project.

#R: how your Java finds your XML

R.layout.activity_main and R.id.main aren't variables you wrote. On every build, Android generates a class named R holding a number for every resource. Add res/layout/settings.xml and R.layout.settings exists after the next build. Give a view android:id="@+id/main" and R.id.main appears. The + in @+id means "create this ID if it doesn't exist yet."

That's also why one typo in an XML file can turn your Java red. If the resources fail to compile, R isn't regenerated, and every line that uses it suddenly can't find its symbol. Fix the XML first; the Java errors vanish with it.

#activity_main.xml: what the screen looks like

Layouts describe a screen in XML. Each tag is a View (something visible, like TextView) or a ViewGroup that arranges other views (like ConstraintLayout). Attributes come in three families:

  • android: attributes are built into Android, such as android:text.
  • app: attributes come from libraries, such as ConstraintLayout's app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf.
  • tools: attributes only affect the preview in Android Studio and are stripped from the real app.

The layout editor has three modes at its top right: Code, Split, and Design. Use Split while you're learning, so you can type XML on one side and watch the preview change on the other.

#res/values: text, colors, and themes

  • strings.xml holds the app's text. The template defines one string, app_name.
  • colors.xml holds named colors; you start with black and white.
  • themes/themes.xml sets the app's overall look. The template's theme is based on Theme.Material3.DayNight.NoActionBar: Material Design 3 styling, automatic dark mode, and no title bar.

Week 3 is built on these files.

#AndroidManifest.xml: the app's ID card

Before Android runs a line of your code, it reads the manifest:

  • android:label is the name under the app icon. It points at @string/app_name, so you rename the app in strings.xml, not here.
  • android:icon and android:roundIcon point at the launcher icons in res/mipmap.
  • Every Activity needs its own <activity> tag. Forget one and the app crashes the moment you try to open that screen.
  • The MAIN action plus the LAUNCHER category mark the Activity that opens when someone taps the icon.
  • android:exported="true" lets the home-screen launcher, which is a different app, start this Activity.

#Gradle: the recipe for building your app

Gradle compiles your Java, packs in your resources, pulls in libraries, and produces an APK, the file that gets installed on a phone. New projects write the recipe in Kotlin DSL files (.kts), even for Java apps. You don't need to know Kotlin to read them; treat them as settings.

The one you'll open most is build.gradle.kts (Module :app). Trimmed to the parts that matter:

  • applicationId is the app's unique ID on a phone and on Google Play.
  • minSdk = 24 means the app installs on Android 7.0 and newer.
  • compileSdk and targetSdk are the newest Android version you build against. Your numbers may be higher, and newer versions of Android Studio may write it as compileSdk { version = release(36) }; both mean the same thing.
  • versionName is the version people see. versionCode is a whole number that must go up with every release.

The libs. names come from the version catalog, gradle/libs.versions.toml, which keeps every library's name and version in one place. Dashes in the catalog become dots in the build file, so android-application in the catalog is libs.plugins.android.application here.

⚠️ Watch out

Edit a Gradle file and a yellow bar appears saying the files have changed. Click Sync Now before you build. Building with unsynced Gradle files is a classic cause of Cannot resolve symbol errors that make no sense.

#What happens when you press Run

If a change doesn't seem to show up, the build probably failed quietly at the first step. Open the Build window at the bottom and read the first red line.

Next to Run sit the Apply Changes buttons, which push small edits without reinstalling. They're quick, but when anything looks odd, a plain Run is the reliable choice.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You change app_name in strings.xml to Pocket Planner. Which file connects that string to the label under the app icon?

  • The Activity never mentions the app's name; it only shows a layout.

  • Its android:label="@string/app_name" attribute points at the string, so the label changes without editing the manifest itself.

  • That file holds applicationId, the app's hidden unique ID, not the name people see.

Show answer

B. Its android:label="@string/app_name" attribute points at the string, so the label changes without editing the manifest itself.

2You add a new TextView with android:id="@+id/score", but another XML file has a typo and the build fails. Why does R.id.score turn red in your Java?

  • Any layout can define IDs.

  • Fix the XML typo, rebuild, and R.id.score appears.

  • The + belongs in the XML only, where it means "create this ID".

Show answer

B. Fix the XML typo, rebuild, and R.id.score appears.

3A classmate creates a second Activity class but never adds it to the manifest. What happens?

  • Java compiles it happily; the compiler doesn't check the manifest for you.

  • Android Studio's New > Activity wizard adds it for you, but a class you create by hand isn't registered anywhere.

  • Android refuses to start an Activity the manifest doesn't list, so the crash comes at runtime.

Show answer

C. Android refuses to start an Activity the manifest doesn't list, so the crash comes at runtime.

4Who calls onCreate() in MainActivity?

  • Android apps don't have a main() you write.

  • Gradle builds and installs the app, but it doesn't run your code.

  • The system creates the Activity and calls its lifecycle methods for you.

Show answer

C. The system creates the Activity and calls its lifecycle methods for you.

Key takeaways

  • java holds code, res holds layouts, text, colors, and images, manifests describes the app, and Gradle Scripts build it.
  • Android calls your Activity's methods; onCreate() runs first and is where you pick the layout with setContentView.
  • R is generated from your resources, so a broken XML file breaks every R. reference in your Java.
  • Every Activity must be listed in the manifest, and the one with MAIN and LAUNCHER opens from the icon.
  • After any Gradle edit, click Sync Now before building.

#Further reading

  • Projects overview (opens in a new tab): Google's map of every folder and file in a project.
  • App manifest overview (opens in a new tab): what else the manifest declares, such as permissions.
  • The activity lifecycle (opens in a new tab): the full story behind the state diagram above, for when you reach Week 4.

What you'll learn

  • Rename an app through strings.xml and see the new name under its icon.
  • Define your own colors in colors.xml and use them in a layout.
  • Replace hardcoded text with @string/ references and add a second TextView positioned below the first.
  • Explain why MainActivity.java doesn't need to change when the layout does.

The template's white screen with "Hello World!" is the same for every Android developer on the planet. By the end of this build, yours will have your name under the icon, a big two-line greeting, and colors you picked. Here's the target, drawn in HTML so you can see it before you start (on the phone it'll be the real thing):

Along the way you'll touch the manifest's label, three resource files, and the layout: the same tour as the notes, but with your hands on the keyboard.

#Step 1: Create the project

Start a new Empty Views Activity project (File > New > New Project) with these settings:

  • Name: Week1Hello
  • Language: Java
  • Minimum SDK: API 24
  • Build configuration language: Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts)

Wait for the Gradle sync to finish, then press Run once before changing anything. If the unchanged template runs, any problem later is something you typed, which makes it much easier to find.

#Step 2: Rename the app and write your text

The name under the icon comes from the manifest's android:label="@string/app_name", so the place to change it is app > res > values > strings.xml. While it's open, add the two lines of text for the screen:

Use your own name. Look closely at I\'m: an apostrophe inside an Android string has to be escaped with a backslash. Leave the backslash out and Android Studio flags the line as an error.

#Step 3: Pick your colors

Open res > values > colors.xml. Keep the template's two colors and add yours. Colors are written #AARRGGBB (alpha, then red, green, blue), where FF alpha means fully opaque:

Android Studio draws a little color square in the left margin beside each line. Click one to pick a color visually instead of typing hex.

💡 Tip

Resource names may only contain lowercase letters, digits, and underscores. c4t_navy works; C4T-Navy won't compile.

#Step 4: Use them in the layout

Open res > layout > activity_main.xml in Split mode. Three changes:

  1. Give the root ConstraintLayout a background color.
  2. Point the existing TextView at your greeting, give it an ID, and make it big and gold.
  3. Add a second TextView underneath for the subtitle.

Replace the whole file with this:

Watch the preview as you paste: the screen turns navy and both lines appear. Here's what each change does.

  • android:background="@color/c4t_navy" paints the whole screen. The @color/ prefix means "look this name up in colors.xml."
  • android:text="@string/greeting" replaces the hardcoded "Hello World!". Keeping text in strings.xml is how real apps get translated: add a second strings.xml for another language and the layout never changes.
  • sp (scale-independent pixels) is the unit for text, because it grows when someone picks a larger font in their phone's settings. dp is for everything else, like the 12dp gap.
  • The subtitle is pinned to the parent's left and right edges, which centers it, and its top hangs from the bottom of greetingText. The reference @id/greetingText has no + because that ID already exists.

⚠️ Watch out

Keep android:id="@+id/main" on the root layout. MainActivity.java calls findViewById(R.id.main) to add the system-bar padding, so if that ID disappears, the build fails with error: cannot find symbol pointing at R.id.main.

#Step 5: Leave MainActivity.java alone (and know why)

Open MainActivity.java and you'll find nothing to change. It already calls setContentView(R.layout.activity_main), so it shows whatever that layout describes. That split is the whole point of Android's View system: what the screen looks like lives in XML, and what it does lives in Java. In Week 4 you'll write Java that changes these views while the app runs, which is why both text views now have IDs.

#Step 6: Run it

Choose your emulator or phone and click Run. You should see:

  • A navy screen.
  • Hi, I'm Maya! (with your name) in large, bold gold text in the middle.
  • This is my first Android app. in white just below it.

Press the home button and open the app drawer: your app is now called Hello C4T. If the old name lingers, uninstall the app (long-press the icon, then Uninstall or App info > Uninstall) and run again; some launchers cache labels.

#Step 7: Compare the preview with the device

Switch the layout editor to Design and hold it up against the real screen. They should match. If the preview looks wrong but the device is right, click the refresh arrow above the preview; it sometimes lags behind your typing.

#If something goes wrong

What you see Likely cause
error: resource string/greting (aka com.example.week1hello:string/greting) not found. A typo between the name in strings.xml and the @string/ reference
A red error on a string containing an apostrophe I'm written without the backslash in strings.xml
The subtitle sits at the very top of the screen The second TextView is missing app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf
The old screen still appears The build failed; open the Build window and read the first error

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the layout say android:text="@string/greeting" instead of android:text="Hi, I'm Maya!"?

  • It compiles fine; Android Studio just shows a yellow warning.

  • A values-es/strings.xml with the same names would give you a Spanish app, layouts untouched.

  • Speed isn't the reason; organization and translation are.

Show answer

B. A values-es/strings.xml with the same names would give you a Spanish app, layouts untouched.

2The greeting uses 32sp, and the gap below it uses 12dp. What would change if the greeting used 32dp instead?

  • sp follows the phone's text-size preference; dp doesn't, which hurts people who need bigger text.

  • dp and sp are the same size at the default font setting.

  • dp is a valid unit; Android Studio only warns about it for text.

Show answer

A. sp follows the phone's text-size preference; dp doesn't, which hurts people who need bigger text.

3You delete android:id="@+id/main" from the root layout to tidy up. What happens on the next build?

  • Many IDs are optional, but this one is used by Java code.

  • The inset code calls findViewById(R.id.main), and that symbol no longer exists.

  • The background comes from android:background, not from the ID.

Show answer

B. The inset code calls findViewById(R.id.main), and that symbol no longer exists.

Key takeaways

  • The name under the icon is app_name in strings.xml, reached through the manifest's android:label.
  • @string/name and @color/name look values up in resource files, so one edit changes every screen that uses them.
  • Use sp for text sizes and dp for everything else.
  • MainActivity shows whatever its layout describes, so design changes don't need Java changes.
  • Keep @+id/main on the root layout of every Empty Views Activity project.

#Ideas to make it more yours

  • Add a third line with your favorite app or game, using a new string and android:textStyle="italic".
  • Change c4t_gold to a color you like and watch both the preview and the device update.
  • Move the greeting a third of the way down the screen by adding app:layout_constraintVertical_bias="0.3" to it.

#Further reading

  • String resources (opens in a new tab): escaping apostrophes and quotes, plus plurals for "1 item" versus "2 items".
  • More resource types (opens in a new tab): colors, dimensions, and the other values you can keep in res/values.
  • Run apps on the Android Emulator (opens in a new tab): emulator controls such as rotating the screen and taking screenshots.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick the right type (int, double, boolean, String) and predict what integer division does.
  • Use String methods, compare strings with .equals(), and turn typed text into numbers without crashing.
  • Write methods with if/else, for, and while.
  • Build a class with private fields, a constructor, and methods, then extend it the way MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity.
  • Pass a lambda to a method, the same trick Android uses for button taps.

Here's a tip calculator with a bug. Read it, guess the tip on a $40 bill, then look at what it actually prints:

Zero dollars. No error, no warning, just a wrong answer. By the end of the second section you'll know which two numbers caused it.

Every Android app in this class is Java underneath the XML, and Java is strict: every variable has a fixed type, every statement ends in a semicolon, and the compiler refuses code it can't make sense of. That's annoying for about a week. Then it starts saving you, because it catches mistakes before your app ever reaches a phone.

Each program on this page runs right here, with its real output underneath. To run one yourself, save it in a file named after its class (TipBug.java for public class TipBug), then type javac TipBug.java and java TipBug.

#Every variable has a type, and it never changes

You declare a Java variable with its type, and from then on it can only hold that kind of value:

Type Holds Example
int whole numbers up to about 2.1 billion int lives = 3;
long bigger whole numbers (note the L) long ms = 3_000_000_000L;
double decimals double price = 4.99;
boolean true or false boolean isMuted = false;
char one character, in single quotes char grade = 'A';
String text, in double quotes String player = "Maya";

final turns a variable into a constant: assign it once, and the compiler blocks any later change. The underscores in 3_000_000_000L are just for your eyes; Java ignores them.

#Why 15 / 100 is zero

When both sides of / are int, Java does integer division: it divides and throws away everything after the decimal point. 15 / 100 is 0.15, which becomes 0, and 0 * 40.0 is 0.0. That's the tip bug.

Predict all five lines before you read the output:

Make either side a double and you get the decimal answer, either by writing 2.0 or with a cast like (double) 7. Casting the other way, (int) 9.99, chops off the decimal rather than rounding, so it gives 9. The % operator gives the remainder, handy for "is this number even?" checks. The tip fix is 15.0 / 100 * bill, or better, bill * 0.15.

#Strings are objects with methods

String is a class, not a basic type, so every string comes with methods you call with a dot:

  • Strings are immutable: trim() and toUpperCase() hand back new strings and leave the original alone.
  • substring(7, 14) starts at index 7 and stops before 14. Indexes start at 0.
  • contains("Droid") is false because comparisons care about capital letters.
  • Once a String is involved, + means "join", working left to right. That's why "Score: " + 3 + 4 gives Score: 34, not Score: 7.
  • String.format fills in %s (a string), %d (a whole number), and %.1f (a decimal to 1 place); %% prints a percent sign.

⚠️ Watch out

Compare strings with .equals(), never ==. The == operator asks whether two variables point at the same object in memory, not whether the text matches. It sometimes appears to work, because Java reuses identical string literals, which makes the bug harder to catch when user input arrives and it suddenly doesn't.

#Turning typed text into numbers

Everything a user types into an Android text box arrives as a String, even digits. Integer.parseInt() and Double.parseDouble() convert text to numbers, and they crash on anything that isn't a clean number:

Read the first line of that error: NumberFormatException: For input string: "12 apples". In an app, that exception closes the app in front of the user. The fix is to catch it with try and catch and fall back to something sensible:

If anything inside try throws a NumberFormatException, Java jumps straight to catch. You'll use this same pattern in Week 4 when you read a number from a text box.

#Methods, decisions, and loops

A method is a named block of code that takes parameters and can return a value. Its declaration lists the return type first: String, double, or void for nothing.

  • Conditions go in parentheses and combine with && (and), || (or), and ! (not).
  • The counting for loop has three parts: start, keep-going test, and step. The for-each loop, for (int s : scores), is simpler when you only need each value.
  • while repeats as long as its condition stays true.
  • Arrays have a fixed size, and scores.length (no parentheses) tells you how many items there are.
  • (double) total / scores.length casts before dividing, which is the integer-division fix from earlier.

These methods are static because main calls them directly without making an object first. Methods in your Android classes usually aren't, for reasons the next section makes clear.

#Classes: blueprints for your own types

A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. Each Pet below has its own name and hunger:

  • Fields (name, hunger) hold each object's data. private means only the class's own methods can touch them, so hunger can never go below zero by accident.
  • The constructor has the class's name and no return type, and new Pet("Rex") calls it. this.name means "this object's field", as opposed to the parameter with the same name.
  • toString() decides what prints when you pass an object to println.
  • The last three lines show that object variables hold references. sameDog and rex are two names for one dog, so playing with sameDog changes rex.

#extends: how MainActivity works

public class MainActivity extends AppCompatActivity uses inheritance: your class gets everything AppCompatActivity already does and replaces only the methods you write. Here's the same shape in miniature:

super.onCreate() runs the parent's version first, which is why Android's onCreate begins with super.onCreate(savedInstanceState). @Override asks the compiler to confirm you're really replacing a parent method. Misspell it as onCreat and you get method does not override or implement a method from a supertype instead of a new method that Android never calls.

#Lambdas: handing Android code to run later

A Button can't know what your app wants to happen when it's tapped. So Android defines an interface, a promise that an object has a certain method, and you hand the button an object that keeps the promise. A lambda like v -> { ... } is the short way to write that object. The template already uses one: (v, insets) -> { ... } is the code Android runs when it learns the system bars' sizes.

This plain-Java version fakes a button so you can watch the idea work:

Setting the listener runs nothing. The lambda's body only runs when tap() calls onClick, and it runs again on every tap. In a real app, Android plays the part of tap():

Notice count is a field (static int count), not a local variable inside main. Java won't let a lambda change a local variable from the method around it; try it and the compiler stops you with local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final. In an Activity, the fix is the same: make the counter a field of the class.

💡 Tip

New Android projects compile Java at the Java 11 language level. Stick to features like the ones on this page in your app code. Newer syntax such as record classes or switch with -> arrows works in your terminal's JDK but fails to compile in an Android project.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? double avg = (90 + 85) / 2; System.out.println(avg);

  • That needs decimal division, but 175 / 2 is two ints.

  • Integer division gives 87 first; storing it in a double just adds .0.

  • A double always prints with a decimal point.

Show answer

B. Integer division gives 87 first; storing it in a double just adds .0.

2A user types yes into a box, and your code gets it as String answer. Which check is reliable?

  • == compares object identity, so text typed at runtime usually fails it.

  • .equals() compares the characters themselves.

  • A single = assigns; it doesn't compare.

Show answer

B. .equals() compares the characters themselves.

3What does System.out.println("Score: " + 3 + 4); print?

  • The additions happen left to right, and the left side is already a String.

  • "Score: " + 3 is "Score: 3", then + 4 joins another character.

  • Joining strings and numbers with + is allowed.

Show answer

B. "Score: " + 3 is "Score: 3", then + 4 joins another character.

4You type protected void onCreat(Bundle savedInstanceState) under @Override in MainActivity. What happens?

  • That's what would happen without @Override: a new method Android never calls.

  • @Override makes the compiler check the name against the parent class, and catches the typo.

  • Nothing renames your methods.

Show answer

B. @Override makes the compiler check the name against the parent class, and catches the typo.

Key takeaways

  • Every Java variable has one type for its whole life; int / int throws the decimals away.
  • Compare strings with .equals(), and join them with +, which works left to right.
  • Integer.parseInt crashes on bad text, so wrap it in try/catch whenever the text came from a user.
  • A class bundles private fields with the methods allowed to change them; new builds an object from it.
  • extends and @Override are how MainActivity customizes AppCompatActivity, and super.onCreate() runs the parent's setup first.
  • A lambda is a piece of code you hand over now and that runs later, which is how buttons call your code.

#Further reading

  • Java language basics (dev.java) (opens in a new tab): Oracle's own tutorial on variables, operators, and control flow.
  • Classes and objects (dev.java) (opens in a new tab): constructors, fields, and methods in more depth.
  • Lambda expressions (dev.java) (opens in a new tab): a careful walk from interfaces to lambdas.

What you'll learn

  • Design a class that keeps its data private and guards it with methods.
  • Write methods that build on each other: countDone() feeds metGoal().
  • Turn data into text with loops, StringBuilder, and the ? : operator.
  • Keep a growing collection of objects in an ArrayList and find the best one.

Most apps boil down to a list of things, each with a little data and a few rules about it. A to-do app has tasks, a music app has songs, a fitness app has workouts. Today you'll write the plain-Java core of one of these: a habit tracker that records which days you did each habit and prints a weekly report. No Android yet. The point is to get comfortable designing a class and using it, because that's the shape of the code behind an Android screen, and in Week 5 you'll put a list just like this one on a phone.

Here's the design. One Habit class holds a habit's data and rules; the HabitTracker program creates several and prints the report:

And here's part of the report you'll end with, where # is a day done and - is a day missed:

Work in one file named HabitTracker.java. After each step, compile and run it with javac HabitTracker.java and java HabitTracker. Every step below shows the whole file so far, with // new marking the lines that step adds, and its real output underneath.

#Step 1: A class to hold one habit

A habit has a name, a weekly goal (how many days you want to do it), and a record of the seven days. A boolean array fits that record: daysDone[0] is Monday, daysDone[6] is Sunday, and every slot starts out false.

Two classes share one file. Only HabitTracker is public, and the file has to be named after it. That's fine for a small program; in an Android project, each class gets its own file.

#Step 2: Record days, safely

Marking a day done means setting one slot to true. But what if a bug, or a user, asks for day 9? Here's what an array does with a slot that doesn't exist:

ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 9 out of bounds for length 7, and "Marked!" never prints. In an app, that's a crash. So markDone checks the day before touching the array. Add three methods to Habit and a test in main that makes two mistakes on purpose, marking Tuesday twice and asking for day 9:

Look at what the class protects you from. Marking Tuesday twice still counts once, because the slot is simply true either way. Day 9 gets a polite message instead of a crash, because the guard returns early. And since daysDone is private, no other code can skip that check by writing into the array directly; the only way in is through markDone.

metGoal() reuses countDone() instead of repeating the counting loop. Small methods that build on each other are easier to test, and a bug fixed in one place is fixed everywhere.

#Step 3: Show the week at a glance

Numbers are fine, but a picture reads faster. Add a list of day names at the top of Habit, and two methods that loop over the week:

Three new pieces of Java:

  • static final on DAY_NAMES: static means one shared copy for every habit (they all use the same day names), and final means it can't be swapped for a different array.
  • condition ? a : b is the ternary operator, a one-line if/else that picks a value. daysDone[i] ? "#" : "-" gives # for a done day and - otherwise.
  • StringBuilder builds text piece by piece. For seven characters, += would work just as well, but you'll meet StringBuilder all over real Java code.

Both loops count with i instead of using for-each, because they need the position (which day) and not just the value.

#Step 4: Track several habits with an ArrayList

An array has a fixed size, but people add and remove habits. An ArrayList grows as you add to it. Put import java.util.ArrayList; at the very top of the file and replace main. Here's the finished program:

What to notice in the new main:

  • ArrayList<Habit> holds only Habit objects; the compiler rejects anything else. The empty <> on the right lets Java fill in the type.
  • ArrayList uses methods where arrays use brackets: add() to put something in, get(0) instead of [0], and size() instead of .length.
  • The "find the best" loop is a pattern worth memorizing: assume the first item is best, then replace it whenever you meet a better one. Because the test is > and not >=, a tie keeps the habit that came first.

⚠️ Watch out

An ArrayList can't hold basic types like int directly. Write ArrayList<Integer>, not ArrayList<int>, which fails with unexpected type. Java converts between int and Integer for you when you add and get values.

#How this connects to Android

In Week 5 you'll show a scrolling list on a phone, and the code behind it has this exact shape: a model class like Habit, an ArrayList of those objects, and a loop-like piece of code that turns each object into a row on screen.

Because the rules live inside Habit, the Android version won't need to re-check day numbers or recount anything. It just calls the methods you wrote today.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is daysDone declared private?

  • private changes who can see a field, not how big it is.

  • Code outside the class can't write daysDone[9] = true and skip the guard.

  • Arrays can be public; it's a design choice, and here a good one.

Show answer

B. Code outside the class can't write daysDone[9] = true and skip the guard.

2After markDone(1) runs twice and markDone(9) once, what does countDone() return if nothing else was marked?

  • Tuesday's slot is just true twice, and day 9 is rejected by the guard.

  • Marking a day again doesn't add a second check mark; the slot is a boolean, not a counter.

  • Day 9 never reaches the array.

Show answer

A. Tuesday's slot is just true twice, and day 9 is rejected by the guard.

3Why does main keep the habits in an ArrayList<Habit> instead of a Habit[] array?

  • Arrays can hold objects; Habit[] would compile.

  • An array's size is fixed when it's created.

  • It keeps them in the order you added them.

Show answer

B. An array's size is fixed when it's created.

Key takeaways

  • Keep a class's data private and change it only through methods that check their inputs.
  • Build small methods on top of each other, like metGoal() using countDone().
  • Loop with an index when you need positions, and with for-each when you only need values.
  • ArrayList grows as you add(), and uses get(i) and size() instead of [i] and .length.
  • To find the best item, start with the first one and replace it whenever a later one beats it.

  • Add int percentDone() that returns how much of the goal is complete, capped at 100. Watch out for integer division.

What you'll learn

  • Choose number types and format output so decimals come out right.
  • Validate text with String methods and early returns.
  • Use while and nested for loops when the number of repeats isn't obvious.
  • Parse user-style input without crashing, using try and catch.
  • Design classes that work together, and pass behavior around with a lambda.

Each exercise is a complete program you can write in one file and run with javac and java. The output it should print is given, so you can check yourself; your code doesn't have to match the solution line for line, but it does have to print the same thing. Every solution runs on this page, so its output appears right under it.

#Warm-up: three predictions

Say what each line prints before you scroll on. Answers are below the list.

  1. System.out.println(10 / 4 * 2.0);
  2. System.out.println("Level " + 2 + 1);
  3. System.out.println("Java".substring(1, 3));

(Answers: 4.0, because 10 / 4 is 2 first; Level 21; and av.)

#Exercise 1: Temperature report

Store these Celsius readings in a double array: 18.5, 31.0, 24.2, 35.6, 9.0. For each one, print the Fahrenheit value to one decimal place (F = C × 9 / 5 + 32). Add (hot) after readings above 30 C and (cold) after readings below 10 C.

Need a hint?

Loop over the array with for-each. Build a label string that starts empty and becomes " (hot)" or " (cold)" with if/else if. String.format("%.1f", value) gives one decimal place.

Show solution

Because c is a double, c * 9 / 5 stays a decimal all the way through. If c were an int, the division by 5 would throw away the fraction.

#Exercise 2: Username rules

Write static boolean isValidUsername(String name) that returns true only when the name is 3 to 15 characters long, has no spaces, and starts with a letter. Test it on maya_codes, jo, 4tomorrow, big bird, android_developer_01, and Sam2026.

Need a hint?

Check one rule at a time and return false the moment a rule fails. name.charAt(0) gives the first character, and Character.isLetter(...) tests it.

Show solution

Returning early keeps each rule on its own short line, and the length check comes first so charAt(0) never runs on an empty string. You'll run the same kind of check on text typed into an Android sign-up screen.

#Exercise 3: Battery drain

A phone starts at 100% and loses 7% each hour. Use a while loop to find how many hours pass before the battery drops below 20%. Then use nested for loops to draw a bar of | characters, one per 10%, for the levels 100, 75, 50, 25, and 0.

Need a hint?

You don't know the number of hours in advance, which is the sign to use while (battery >= 20). For the bars, the outer loop counts down by 25, and the inner loop runs level / 10 times. %3d pads a number to three characters.

Show solution

Integer division does useful work here: 75 / 10 is 7, so 75% gets seven bars. %% prints a literal percent sign, and stripTrailing() removes the space left after 0% when its bar is empty.

#Exercise 4: Read an age safely

In Week 4 you'll read numbers from a text box, where people type anything. Write static int parseAge(String text) that trims the text, converts it to an int, and returns -1 if the text isn't a number or the age is outside 0 to 120. Test it on "15", " 42 ", "fifteen", "-3", "200", and "".

Need a hint?

Put Integer.parseInt(text.trim()) inside try, and return -1 in a catch (NumberFormatException e). The range check goes after a successful parse, still inside try.

Show solution

"fifteen" and "" both throw NumberFormatException, so they land in catch. "-3" parses fine, which is why the range check is needed too. \" puts a quote mark inside a string.

#Exercise 5: Playlist classes

Create a Song class (title and length in seconds, both private, with getters) and a Playlist class that holds an ArrayList<Song>. Playlist needs add(Song), totalSeconds(), longest(), a static helper formatTime(int seconds) that returns text like 3:05, and print(). Build a "Study Mix" with three songs: Lo-fi Morning (185 s), Rainy Window (242 s), and Focus Mode (207 s).

Need a hint?

formatTime is two integer operations: seconds / 60 for minutes and seconds % 60 for seconds. %02d pads the seconds to two digits. longest() uses the "assume the first is best" loop from the habit tracker.

Show solution

formatTime is static because it doesn't use any playlist's data; it only converts a number. One weakness: longest() crashes on an empty playlist, so a real app would check songs.isEmpty() first.

#Exercise 6: A button that calls you back

Fake the way an Android button works. Write an interface OnTapListener with one method, void onTap(int tapNumber), and a class TapButton with setOnTapListener(OnTapListener listener) and tap(). Each tap() counts the tap and calls the listener with the count, but if no listener has been set yet, tap() does nothing at all (no count, no crash).

In main, tap once before setting a listener, then set one with a lambda that prints Tap n, adding : combo! on every third tap, and tap five more times:

Need a hint?

Store the listener in a private field that starts as null. At the top of tap(), if (listener == null) { return; }. The lambda takes one parameter, n -> { ... }, and n % 3 == 0 spots every third tap.

Show solution

The first tap() returns early, so nothing prints and the count stays at 0. Without the null check, it would crash with a NullPointerException, which is also what happens in Android if you call a method on a view that findViewById couldn't find. The lambda's code is stored, not run, until tap() calls onTap.

#Challenge: Savings accounts

Write an Account class with an owner, a balance, a withdraw(double amount) method that returns false (and changes nothing) for amounts that are zero, negative, or more than the balance, and a toString() like Maya: $30.00.

Then write SavingsAccount extends Account with an interest rate, an addInterest() method, and a limit of two successful withdrawals. Override withdraw and toString, and use super in both. Put both classes in Bank.java, above a public class Bank whose main runs these lines:

It should print:

Need a hint?

The subclass constructor must start with super(owner, balance). Make balance protected so addInterest() can change it. In the overridden withdraw, check the withdrawal limit first, then let super.withdraw(amount) do the balance checks, and only count the withdrawal if it returned true.

Show solution

super(owner, balance) has to be the first line of the subclass constructor. balance is protected so the subclass can add interest, while owner stays private. The overridden withdraw adds one new rule and hands everything else to super.withdraw, so the balance checks live in one place. That's the same relationship your MainActivity has with AppCompatActivity: add what's new, and let the parent do the rest.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe a screen as a tree of views and give every view a width and a height.
  • Choose dp or sp for a size, and know why raw pixels are avoided.
  • Stack views with LinearLayout and split space with layout_weight.
  • Position views with ConstraintLayout so the screen stretches cleanly on any phone.
  • Configure the four everyday views and pull their values from res/values.

Your profile screen looks perfect on the Pixel emulator. Then a classmate runs it on a small phone and the email address runs off the right edge, and on a tablet everything huddles in the top-left corner. Nothing is wrong with the Java; the layout just described positions when it should have described relationships. This week is about writing layouts that bend instead of break.

#Every screen is a tree of views

Everything you can see is a View: a piece of text, a button, an image. Containers that arrange other views are ViewGroups, and they nest, so every screen is a tree. Here's the sign-up screen from the next section, drawn as its tree:

Android measures the tree from the top down: each parent tells its children how much room there is, and each child answers with how big it wants to be. A child says that with two required attributes, android:layout_width and android:layout_height, each set to one of:

  • wrap_content: just big enough for what's inside.
  • match_parent: as big as the parent allows.
  • A fixed size such as 48dp.

Leave one out and Android Studio underlines the tag in red. Run it anyway and the app crashes when that screen loads, with You must supply a layout_width attribute.

#dp and sp: sizes that mean the same on every phone

Android screens range from about 160 pixels per inch to well over 400. Size a button in pixels and it's a fingertip on one phone and a grain of rice on another. So Android measures in two units of its own:

  • dp (density-independent pixels) is roughly the same physical size on every screen. Use it for widths, heights, margins, and padding. A comfortable touch target is at least 48dp tall.
  • sp (scale-independent pixels) is dp that also follows the user's font-size setting. Use it only for text sizes.

#LinearLayout: one row or one column

A LinearLayout lines its children up in a single column or row, set by android:orientation. It's the simplest container there is, and perfect for forms and rows of buttons:

The two buttons use weights. A width of 0dp plus a layout_weight tells the row, "ignore my natural size and give me a share of the space." Weights of 1 and 1 split the row in half. Weights of 1 and 2 give Join two of three shares. Drag the slider to see the split change (this is a browser imitation, but the arithmetic is the same):

Two pairs of attributes trip everyone up at first:

  • android:gravity positions a view's content inside it, like text inside a button. android:layout_gravity asks the parent to position the view itself.
  • Padding is space inside a view's border; margin is space outside it.

The root LinearLayout keeps android:id="@+id/main" so the template's MainActivity still compiles.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't put android:padding on the root layout in an Empty Views Activity project. The template's inset code in MainActivity calls setPadding() on that view while the app runs, which replaces your padding with the system-bar sizes. Use margins on the children, or pad an inner layout instead.

#ConstraintLayout: place views by their relationships

Nesting rows inside columns inside rows gets messy fast. ConstraintLayout, the template's default root, keeps every view in one flat layer and places each one by tying its edges to the parent or to other views:

Read each constraint as a sentence. app:layout_constraintStart_toEndOf="@id/photo" says "my start edge sits against the photo's end edge." Drawn out, the four views hang off each other like this:

The rules that matter most:

  • Every view needs at least one horizontal and one vertical constraint. Without them Android Studio warns This view is not constrained, and on the phone the view jumps to the top-left corner.
  • A width of 0dp means match constraints: stretch to fill the space between the start and end constraints. That's how the name fills the gap beside the photo and wraps a long name instead of running off the screen, which is the fix for the phone in this lesson's first paragraph.
  • Constrain both sides and the view centers between them. app:layout_constraintHorizontal_bias="0.3" slides it 30% of the way across instead of 50%.
  • Use start and end rather than left and right. They flip automatically for right-to-left languages like Arabic and Hebrew.

In Design view you can drag the small circles on a view's edges to make constraints, but always check the XML afterwards; a missing constraint is far easier to spot in text.

#The four everyday views

TextView shows text. Useful attributes: android:text, android:textSize, android:textColor, android:textStyle (bold, italic), android:gravity, and android:maxLines with android:ellipsize="end" to cut long text off with "...". Use tools:text for placeholder text that only appears in the preview.

Button is a tappable view with text. In a Material 3 project, a plain <Button> tag is automatically turned into a Material button with rounded corners and the theme's main color. Change its color with app:backgroundTint; android:background won't work on it. Tapping does nothing until Java listens for it, which is next week.

ImageView displays a picture. Prefer app:srcCompat over android:src, because it supports vector images on every Android version. Always set android:contentDescription, which screen readers announce for blind users (use @null for purely decorative images). android:scaleType decides how the image fits its box: fitCenter shows all of it, and centerCrop fills the box and trims the edges. To add an image, copy a .png or .jpg into res/drawable (lowercase name, no spaces or dashes), or make an icon with right-click res > New > Vector Asset.

EditText is a text box. android:hint shows grey placeholder text. android:inputType picks the keyboard: textEmailAddress adds an @ key, number shows a number pad, phone shows a dial pad, and textPassword hides what you type. android:autofillHints (like name, emailAddress, or password) lets the phone's autofill help; for a field that should never be autofilled, such as a note, set android:importantForAutofill="no" instead.

#Resources: one place for text, colors, and sizes

Neither layout above hardcodes a value. Each @string/, @color/, and @dimen/ points into res/values. Here are the strings they need, in strings.xml:

The template has no dimensions file, so make one: right-click res/values, choose New > Values Resource File, and name it dimens:

Colors work the same way in colors.xml, as you saw in Week 1. Why go to the trouble?

  • Consistency: change space_medium once and every screen that uses it updates.
  • Translation: a values-es/strings.xml file with the same names gives you a Spanish app with no layout changes.
  • Variants: values-night colors for dark mode, or bigger dimens for tablets, are picked automatically by the phone.

💡 Tip

Android Studio highlights hardcoded text in yellow. Put the cursor on it, press Alt + Enter (Option + Return on macOS), and choose Extract string resource. It writes the entry in strings.xml and rewrites the attribute for you.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A row has two buttons, both with layout_width="0dp". One has layout_weight="2" and the other layout_weight="1". How is the row split?

  • That's what equal weights do.

  • There are three shares in total, and the first button takes two of them.

  • Weights are shares of the leftover space, not sizes in dp.

Show answer

B. There are three shares in total, and the first button takes two of them.

2In a ConstraintLayout, a button has app:layout_constraintTop_toBottomOf="@id/title" and no other constraints. Where does it appear on the phone?

  • Centering needs both a start and an end constraint.

  • It has a vertical constraint but no horizontal one, so it falls back to x = 0.

  • Dragged positions are tools: attributes, which only exist in the preview.

Show answer

B. It has a vertical constraint but no horizontal one, so it falls back to x = 0.

3You want the word "Join" centered inside a wide button. Which attribute goes on the button?

  • gravity positions the content inside the view.

  • That asks the parent to move the whole button, not its text.

  • Padding takes a size like 8dp, not a position.

Show answer

A. gravity positions the content inside the view.

4Which inputType should a text box for a phone number use?

  • That shows a full keyboard, which slows people down.

  • A number pad works, but it has no + or other dialing symbols.

  • It opens a dial pad with the symbols phone numbers need.

Show answer

C. It opens a dial pad with the symbols phone numbers need.

Key takeaways

  • A screen is a tree of views inside ViewGroups, and every view needs layout_width and layout_height.
  • Use dp for sizes and spacing, sp only for text, and make touch targets at least 48dp tall.
  • LinearLayout stacks in one direction; 0dp plus layout_weight splits the space by shares.
  • In ConstraintLayout, every view needs a horizontal and a vertical constraint, and 0dp stretches between them.
  • Pull text, colors, and sizes from res/values so one edit updates every screen, and translation and dark mode come for free.

#Further reading

  • Layouts in views (opens in a new tab): Google's overview of the view tree, IDs, and layout parameters.
  • Build a responsive UI with ConstraintLayout (opens in a new tab): every constraint type, plus chains, guidelines, and barriers for when you outgrow the basics.
  • App resources overview (opens in a new tab): the full list of qualifiers, like -night and -es, that Android uses to pick resources.
