What you'll learn

  • Combine a ConstraintLayout page with a LinearLayout inside a MaterialCardView.
  • Create a vector icon with Vector Asset Studio and tint it from a color resource.
  • Keep every string, color, and size in res/values, named by role.
  • Line views up by constraining them to another view instead of the parent.

Business cards make a perfect first real screen: small enough to finish in one class, but with every ingredient of a production layout. Here's what you're building, imitated in HTML so you can see the goal (yours will be real Android views):

The note box and button won't do anything yet. In Week 4 you'll bring them to life with Java, and they get IDs today so that's easy.

#Step 1: Create the project

New project, Empty Views Activity, named Week3BusinessCard. Choose Java, API 24 as the minimum SDK, and Kotlin DSL for the build files, then let the sync finish.

#Step 2: Make an avatar icon

You need an image, and Android Studio can draw one for you:

  1. Right-click res and choose New > Vector Asset.
  2. Leave Asset type on Clip art. Click the icon next to Clip art, search for account circle, select it, and click OK.
  3. Change Name to ic_avatar.
  4. Click Next, then Finish.

You now have res/drawable/ic_avatar.xml. It's a vector drawable: the picture is stored as shapes instead of pixels, so it stays sharp at any size and takes almost no space.

#Step 3: The resource files

Text first. Replace res/values/strings.xml (use your own details if you like):

Then the palette. Keep black and white in res/values/colors.xml and add the rest:

These names describe each color's job (brand, divider), not its look (green, light_grey). That pays off the day you rebrand: change brand to purple and the name still makes sense, while a color called green holding purple would confuse everyone.

Finally, create res/values/dimens.xml with right-click values > New > Values Resource File:

#Step 4: Plan the tree, then write the layout

Before typing XML, sketch the tree. Three big blocks sit on the page, and the card holds a column of its own:

Open res/layout/activity_main.xml in Split view and replace everything with this. Read it through once before running; the explanation follows.

#How the layout fits together

Two containers, each doing what it's best at. The outer ConstraintLayout places the three big blocks. Inside the card, a vertical LinearLayout stacks six views, which is far simpler than writing constraints for every line of text.

The card. MaterialCardView comes from the Material Components library, which the template already includes through implementation(libs.material) in your app's Gradle file, so there's nothing to add. Its app:card... attributes set the color, corner radius, and shadow. Underneath, a card is a FrameLayout, which piles its children on top of each other, so it gets exactly one child: the LinearLayout that does the stacking.

Width 0dp, constrained to the card. The card stretches between the screen edges minus its 24dp margins. The note field and button use the same 0dp trick, but they constrain to @id/card instead of the parent, so their edges line up exactly with the card's. Change the card's margins later and everything stays aligned.

Centering inside the card. android:gravity="center_horizontal" on the LinearLayout centers the avatar, name, and title. The email and location are match_parent wide, so they fill the row and their text starts at the left edge, like a printed card.

A divider from a plain View. A View that's 1dp tall with a background color is the simplest line you can draw.

The image. app:srcCompat loads the vector drawable on every Android version, and app:tint recolors it brand green. TalkBack, Android's screen reader, reads the contentDescription aloud.

The note field. textCapSentences|textMultiLine combines two input types with |: the keyboard capitalizes the first letter, and the box grows as you type more lines. importantForAutofill="no" tells autofill there's nothing to suggest. The explicit text and hint colors keep it readable in dark mode, since this page stays light either way.

⚠️ Watch out

If the avatar line turns red with Cannot resolve symbol '@drawable/ic_avatar', the vector asset was saved under another name. Check res/drawable, then either rename the file (right-click > Refactor > Rename) or change the reference to match.

#Step 5: Run it

Run the app. You should see a light grey-blue page with a white card near the top: a green person icon, Maya Patel in bold, the green title under it, a thin divider, and the email and location in grey. Below the card sits a text field with the hint Add a note about this contact, then a full-width green Save contact button.

Tap the text field: the keyboard opens, and the first letter you type is capitalized. Tap the button: it ripples and does nothing else, which is correct for now. Next week, that tap will run code:

#Step 6: Prove the resources are doing their job

  1. In colors.xml, change brand to #FF6A1B9A (purple) and run again. The icon, the title, and the button all change together.
  2. In dimens.xml, change avatar_size to 128dp. The avatar grows, and everything below it moves down to make room.
  3. Open Design view and pick a different device from the toolbar dropdown, such as a small phone or a tablet. The card always stretches to fit, because its width comes from constraints, not a fixed number.

Put the values back, or keep the ones you like, before moving on.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The note field and button use app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="@id/card" instead of "parent". What does that buy you?

  • It looks the same today, but not after you change the card's margins.

  • They follow the card, so one margin edit moves all three blocks together.

  • They're still children of the ConstraintLayout; they're only positioned relative to the card.

Show answer

B. They follow the card, so one margin edit moves all three blocks together.

2Why does the card contain a LinearLayout instead of the six views directly?

  • MaterialCardView is a FrameLayout underneath, which overlaps its children.

  • They can hold any view; they just don't arrange several of them.

  • Tinting belongs to the ImageView and works in any container.

Show answer

A. MaterialCardView is a FrameLayout underneath, which overlaps its children.

3You change brand from green to purple in colors.xml. What changes on screen?

  • The button isn't the only view that uses @color/brand.

  • All three refer to @color/brand, so one edit recolors them together.

  • The layout already points at the name, and the name now holds purple.

Show answer

B. All three refer to @color/brand, so one edit recolors them together.

Key takeaways

  • Use ConstraintLayout for the page and a LinearLayout wherever a simple stack is clearer.
  • Vector Asset Studio makes crisp icons, and app:tint colors them from a resource.
  • Name colors by job, like brand and divider, and keep every size in dimens.xml.
  • Constraining to another view's edges keeps blocks aligned when things change.
  • Give views IDs now if Java will need them later.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a phone number line and a small ic_email vector icon next to the email, inside a horizontal LinearLayout.
  • Give the card a thin brand-colored border with app:strokeColor and app:strokeWidth.
  • Make a values-night/colors.xml so the page turns dark in dark mode, then check that the note field's text and hint colors still read well against it.

#Further reading

  • Create a card-based layout (opens in a new tab): cards in the View system, with corner and elevation attributes.
  • Add multi-density vector graphics (opens in a new tab): everything Vector Asset Studio can import, including your own SVG files.
  • Linear layout (opens in a new tab): weights, orientation, and gravity in Google's own words.

What you'll learn

  • Move hardcoded values into string, color, and dimension resources.
  • Split a row by weights and place views with constraints and bias.
  • Pick the right inputType, autofillHints, and scaleType for a job.
  • Diagnose a view that looks right in Design view but jumps on the phone.

Do these in a scratch project (an Empty Views Activity named Week3Practice works well) or in your business-card project. Each solution is XML you paste into activity_main.xml or the resource file it names. Keep the editor in Split view so every change shows up in the preview as you type.

Unless an exercise says otherwise, put views inside the template's root ConstraintLayout and keep its android:id="@+id/main".

#Warm-up: name the attribute

Answer from memory, then check against the notes.

  1. Which attribute centers the text inside a button?
  2. Which width makes a view stretch between its start and end constraints?
  3. Which unit belongs on android:textSize?

(Answers: android:gravity, 0dp, and sp.)

#Exercise 1: Move everything into resources

This TextView works, but every value is hardcoded. Move the text, the color, and both sizes into strings.xml, colors.xml, and dimens.xml, then update the view to use them.

Need a hint?

Four values, three files: one <string>, one <color>, and two <dimen> entries. Then swap each value in the view for @string/..., @color/..., or @dimen/.... Alt + Enter on the text can do the string for you.

Show solution

Add one entry to each resource file, inside its <resources> tag:

Then the view becomes:

The yellow hardcoded-text warning disappears. Extract string resource handles strings automatically; colors and dimensions you move by hand.

#Exercise 2: A row of equal buttons

Make a horizontal row of three buttons, Easy, Medium, and Hard, that always split the screen width into three equal parts with 8dp gaps between them. Then change it so Medium is twice as wide as each of the others.

Need a hint?

A horizontal LinearLayout inside the root does the splitting. Every button needs layout_width="0dp" and a layout_weight. Margins on the middle button create both gaps.

Show solution

Place this inside the root ConstraintLayout:

Add easy, medium, and hard to strings.xml. For the second part, change the middle button's android:layout_weight to 2: the row is now four shares, and Medium takes two. Widths must be 0dp for weights to divide the space exactly. With wrap_content, the weights only share out whatever's left after each button takes its natural width, so "Medium" would end up a little wider than intended.

#Exercise 3: Corners and bias

Using only constraints, put a small v1.0 label in the bottom-right corner, 16dp from both edges. Then add a headline that's centered horizontally but sits 30% of the way down the screen instead of in the middle.

Need a hint?

A corner needs just two constraints. The headline needs all four, which centers it both ways; one more attribute shifts it vertically. A bias of 0.5 is the middle.

Show solution

The version label hugs a corner, so bottom and end are enough. The headline is pulled equally from all four sides, which centers it, and layout_constraintVertical_bias="0.3" slides it from the default 0.5 up to 0.3. A bias of 0 pins it to the top; 1 pins it to the bottom.

#Exercise 4: A login form with the right keyboards

Build a login screen with an email field, a password field, and a full-width Log in button, stacked vertically. The email field should bring up a keyboard with an @ key, the password should be hidden as you type, and both should work with the phone's autofill. Use a LinearLayout as the root this time.

Need a hint?

Two attributes per field do the work: inputType picks the keyboard and masking, and autofillHints tells autofill what goes there. Remember where padding is safe in an Empty Views Activity project.

Show solution

The padding sits on the inner LinearLayout, because the template's MainActivity overwrites the root's padding with the system-bar sizes. No app: namespace is needed, since nothing here uses a library attribute. Run it and tap each field to see the two different keyboards.

#Exercise 5: A banner photo

Copy any landscape photo into res/drawable and name it banner.jpg (lowercase letters, digits, and underscores only). Show it across the full width of the screen at the top, 160dp tall, filling the area without stretching or squashing the picture. Then try fitCenter and fitXY, and describe the difference.

Need a hint?

Full width in a ConstraintLayout is 0dp with start and end constraints. The attribute that decides how a picture fits its box is android:scaleType, and the value you want fills the box and trims what spills over.

Show solution

The reference is @drawable/banner, without .jpg.

  • centerCrop scales the photo until it covers the whole box, then trims the overflow. No empty space, no distortion.
  • fitCenter shrinks the photo until all of it fits, which leaves empty bands at the sides or the top and bottom.
  • fitXY stretches it to the box's exact shape, which squashes faces and turns circles into ovals. You'll rarely want it for photos.

#Exercise 6: Why is everything in the corner?

A classmate's preview looks fine in Design view, but on the phone both views pile up in the top-left corner, on top of each other. Android Studio shows a red error on each. Explain why, then fix it so the title is centered near the top and the button sits under it.

Need a hint?

Look at the namespace on the position attributes. What happens to tools: attributes when the app is built?

Show solution

The error reads: This view is not constrained. It only has designtime positions, so it will jump to (0,0) at runtime unless you add the constraints. Like every tools: attribute, they only affect the preview and are thrown away in the real app.

Remove them and add real constraints:

Each view now has a horizontal pair (start and end, which centers it) and a vertical constraint, so the phone puts it exactly where the preview does.

What you'll learn

  • Give views an android:id and reach them from Java with findViewById.
  • Respond to a tap with a click listener, a Toast, or an error on the field.
  • Turn typed text into a number without crashing on empty or strange input.
  • Say when each Activity lifecycle method runs.
  • Explain why rotating the phone wipes your fields, and save them with onSaveInstanceState.

Last week's layout had a perfect Button. Tap it now and nothing happens. No error, no crash, nothing. XML can describe a button, but it can't decide what a tap means. Deciding is Java's job, and right now your Java has no idea the button exists.

There's a stranger problem waiting further down. Build a score counter, tap it up to 7, turn the phone sideways, and the score is back to 0. Nothing in your code reset it. By the end of these notes you'll know exactly who did, and how to stop it.

#Give a view an id, then look it up

Think of the layout as a room full of objects and an id as a name tag. Java can only grab an object that wears a tag. You add the tag in XML with android:id; the @+id/ part means "create this id if it doesn't exist yet."

When you build, Android Studio turns every id into a number in a generated class called R, so @+id/greet_button becomes R.id.greet_button. In onCreate, after setContentView, you ask for each view by that number:

findViewById searches only the layout you handed to setContentView. Call it before that line, or pass an id that lives in a different layout file, and it quietly returns null. You won't find out until the next line tries to use the view and the app crashes.

⚠️ Watch out

The crash looks like this in Logcat: java.lang.NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method 'void android.widget.Button.setOnClickListener(android.view.View$OnClickListener)' on a null object reference. It almost always means a misspelled id, an id from another layout, or findViewById called before setContentView.

#Optional: View Binding

View Binding generates a class with one field per view, so you never type an id twice and can't get null for a missing view. Turn it on in app/build.gradle.kts, inside the android { } block, then click Sync Now:

That file is Gradle configuration, not app code, so your app stays pure Java. For activity_main.xml you get a class named ActivityMainBinding, and snake_case ids become camelCase fields:

The course examples use findViewById because it shows every step, but either style is fine in your own projects.

#A click listener is a callback

You don't check the button in a loop asking "tapped yet? tapped yet?" Instead you hand Android a small piece of code and say "run this when it's tapped." That piece of code is a listener: an object with one method, onClick(View v). A Java lambda writes it in one line:

Type Ana and tap, and the TextView reads Hello, Ana! while a small grey message pops up near the bottom. Leave the box empty and a red error icon appears on the field instead. Here's what each line is doing:

  • getText() returns an Editable, not a String, so you add .toString().
  • trim() strips spaces from both ends, so a box with only spaces counts as empty.
  • setError puts the message on the field itself, right where the user is looking.
  • Toast.makeText(context, text, duration) builds a Toast, and .show() displays it. Leave off .show() and nothing appears, with no error to tell you why.

Inside a lambda, this still means the Activity, so Toast.makeText(this, ...) works. In an old-style anonymous class (new View.OnClickListener() { ... }), this would mean the listener, and you'd write MainActivity.this instead.

#Typed text is never a number until you parse it

android:inputType="numberDecimal" shows a number keyboard, but it can't stop a user from leaving the box empty or typing a lone .. You still get a String, and turning it into a double with Double.parseDouble throws a NumberFormatException when the text isn't a number. An exception that nobody catches crashes the app.

So wrap the parse in try/catch. Before you run this, guess which of the six inputs come back as -1:

The surprise is the last line: 1e3 is scientific notation for 1,000, and Java happily accepts it. The number keyboard won't let anyone type an e, but pasted text can sneak one in, which is why you check the parsed value too (a bill can't be negative). Returning -1 works as a "this was bad" signal here because no real bill or percent is negative. In the app, you check for it and call setError instead of crashing.

This is plain Java, so it runs right here on the page. Testing logic outside Android first is a habit worth keeping: if the app shows a wrong number later, you'll know the math was fine and the bug is in the wiring.

#The Activity lifecycle: Android is in charge

Your Activity doesn't just "run." Android moves it through states as the user opens it, covers it with something else, leaves it, and comes back. At every change, Android calls one of your methods so you can react.

Method When Android calls it What to do there
onCreate The Activity object was just created setContentView, find views, attach listeners
onStart It's about to become visible Start things the user can see
onResume It's in front and receiving taps Resume animations, the camera, sensors
onPause Something is partly covering it, or the user is leaving Pause quick work, save a draft
onStop It's no longer visible at all Stop heavy work
onDestroy It's being thrown away Final cleanup

The best way to believe this is to watch it. Override a method, log from it, and filter Logcat by your tag:

Every override must call its super version. Skip it and Android throws a SuperNotCalledException the moment the method runs.

#Why rotation wipes your data

Here's the score counter mystery solved. When the phone rotates, Android destroys your Activity and creates a brand-new one, so the new one can load a landscape layout if you have one. Log all six methods and rotate once, and Logcat shows:

Your int count field lived in the old object, and the old object is gone. The new object starts with count = 0. Views are rebuilt from XML too, with one exception: a view that has an id saves some of its own state. An EditText with an id keeps its typed text. A TextView whose text you changed in code goes back to whatever the XML says.

#Save it in a Bundle before it's destroyed

Just before destroying the old Activity, Android calls onSaveInstanceState and hands you a Bundle, a small box of key-value pairs. Whatever you put in, Android passes to the new Activity's onCreate:

savedInstanceState is null the first time the screen opens, and holds your Bundle after a rotation. Bundles have putInt, putString, putDouble, putBoolean, and matching getters. Keep what you store small: numbers and short strings, not long lists or images.

#Optional: a ViewModel

A ViewModel is an object Android keeps alive across rotation, so there's nothing to pack and unpack:

ViewModelProvider comes from androidx.lifecycle, which the template's AppCompat library already brings in. The catch: a ViewModel survives rotation but not Android killing your app in the background to free memory, while a Bundle survives both. Larger apps often use both.

⚠️ Watch out

Two bugs show up every week in this unit. First, countText.setText(count) with an int compiles, but Android treats the number as a string resource id and crashes with android.content.res.Resources$NotFoundException: String resource ID #0x7. Write setText(String.valueOf(count)). Second, restoring count in onCreate isn't enough on its own: you also have to put it back on screen, or the TextView keeps showing its XML text.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Tapping your new button crashes with a NullPointerException on the line greetButton.setOnClickListener(...). What's the most likely cause?

  • A missing .show() just means no Toast appears; it never crashes, and the listener hasn't even run yet.

  • Right. The crash happens when you call a method on greetButton, so greetButton itself is null.

  • A missing string resource is a build error in the XML, not a crash at this line.

Show answer

B. Right. The crash happens when you call a method on greetButton, so greetButton itself is null.

2Which input makes parseOrMinusOne return -1?

  • trim() removes the spaces first, so it parses as 18.0.

  • That's scientific notation, and Double.parseDouble reads it as 1000.0.

  • A lone decimal point isn't a number, so parseDouble throws and the catch returns -1.

Show answer

C. A lone decimal point isn't a number, so parseDouble throws and the catch returns -1.

3A counter shows 7. It has no onSaveInstanceState. You rotate the phone. What does the screen show?

  • Android only restores views that save their own state, and a TextView changed in code doesn't.

  • Rotation built a brand-new Activity, so the field starts at 0 and the TextView is rebuilt from XML.

  • Nothing here is null; the data is simply lost.

Show answer

B. Rotation built a brand-new Activity, so the field starts at 0 and the TextView is rebuilt from XML.

4The user presses Home, then reopens your app from recent apps a few seconds later. Which methods run when it comes back?

  • onCreate only runs for a new Activity object. Pressing Home stopped yours but didn't destroy it.

  • The stopped Activity is brought back, so your fields are still there.

  • That's what happens when a dialog covering part of the screen goes away. After Home, the Activity was fully stopped.

Show answer

B. The stopped Activity is brought back, so your fields are still there.

Key takeaways

  • Java reaches a view through its android:id, using findViewById after setContentView.
  • A click listener is code you hand to Android to run later; setError and Toast (with .show()) are how you answer the user.
  • Typed text is a String. Parse it inside try/catch and check the result, or bad input crashes the app.
  • Android, not your code, moves an Activity through onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, and onDestroy.
  • Rotation destroys and rebuilds the Activity. Put values in the Bundle in onSaveInstanceState and read them back in onCreate.

#Further reading

  • The Activity lifecycle (opens in a new tab): the official version of the diagram, with what each state means.
  • Save UI states (opens in a new tab): when to use a Bundle, a ViewModel, or saved storage, side by side.
  • View Binding (opens in a new tab): the full setup if you want to try it instead of findViewById.

What you'll learn

  • Test an app's math as plain Java before any Android code exists.
  • Read two EditText fields, validate them, and show the result in a TextView.
  • Store views in fields so more than one method can use them.
  • Keep a result across rotation with onSaveInstanceState, then prove it by breaking it.

A restaurant bill is a perfect first interactive app: two inputs, one button, one answer, and endless ways for a user to type something odd. Here's the finished screen after typing 42.50 and 18 and tapping Calculate:

Leave the bill empty and the bill field shows a red error instead of crashing. Turn the phone sideways and the answer is still there. Every tap follows the same path through the code:

#Step 1: Create the project

In Android Studio choose File > New > New Project > Empty Views Activity, then fill in:

  • Name: Tip Calculator
  • Package name: com.example.tipcalculator
  • Language: Java
  • Minimum SDK: API 24
  • Build configuration language: Kotlin DSL

Wait for the Gradle sync to finish (the progress bar at the bottom goes quiet) before editing anything. Editing during a sync is the fastest way to get confusing red errors that vanish on their own a minute later.

#Step 2: Get the math right first

An Android app has a lot of moving parts: layouts, ids, listeners, the emulator. A bug in the formula would hide among all of them. So start with a plain Java class that only does math. Before you run it, work out 18% of $42.50 in your head (10% is 4.25, so 18% is a bit under double that).

Look at the third line of output. 20% of 23.99 is really 4.798, and %.2f rounds it to two decimal places, which is what money needs. Locale.US is there because formatting follows the phone's language settings: on a phone set to German, the same format prints 7,65 with a comma. Pinning the locale keeps the dollar format predictable.

The formula works. If the app shows a wrong number later, the bug is in how you connected things, not in the math.

#Step 3: Add the strings

Open app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml and replace it with:

The two error messages live here too, so Java can fetch them with getString(R.string.error_bill) instead of hard-coding English inside the code.

#Step 4: Build the layout

Replace app/src/main/res/layout/activity_main.xml. Keep android:id="@+id/main" on the root: the template's Java uses that id to pad the screen away from the status bar.

numberDecimal gives the bill a keyboard with a decimal point. number gives the percent whole digits only. Click the Split or Design button in the top right of the editor: you should see two empty fields with grey hints, a full-width button, and the placeholder sentence.

#Step 5: Wire it up in Java

Replace MainActivity.java with the code below. The top of onCreate is the template's code, unchanged. The new parts are the three fields, the end of onCreate, calculate(), parseOrMinusOne(), and onSaveInstanceState().

Look at where the views are declared. billInput, percentInput, and resultText are fields at the top of the class, not local variables inside onCreate, because calculate() and onSaveInstanceState() need them too. A local variable disappears when onCreate returns. The button stays local because only onCreate touches it.

The return after each setError matters just as much. Without it, the method would keep going and do math with -1, showing a negative tip right under the error.

#Step 6: Run it and check the answers

Click Run 'app' and try each row. Your screen should match:

The first line matches the plain Java test from Step 2 exactly, which is the payoff for running it first.

#Step 7: Prove that rotation works

Calculate a tip, then rotate. On an emulator, use the rotate buttons in the emulator's toolbar; on a phone, switch on auto-rotate in quick settings first. The result is still there.

Now break it on purpose, because seeing the failure is how you know the fix is doing something. Comment out the outState.putString(...) line, run again, calculate, and rotate. The result snaps back to "Enter a bill and a tip percent," while the two typed numbers stay put. That's the rule from the notes in action: an EditText with an id saves its own text, and a TextView you changed in code doesn't. Put the line back.

💡 Tip

Want to watch the rebuild happen? Add Log.d("TipCalc", "onCreate, saved = " + (savedInstanceState != null)); near the top of onCreate and type tag:TipCalc in the Logcat search bar. You'll see saved = false at launch and saved = true after every rotation.

#When it doesn't work

  • App crashes on launch: an id in Java doesn't match the XML. R.id.bill_input must match @+id/bill_input letter for letter.
  • Nothing happens on tap: setOnClickListener is missing, or it's attached to a different view.
  • Red R everywhere in the editor: an XML file has an error, so R couldn't be generated. Fix the XML (look for a red underline) and the Java errors disappear.
  • A negative tip appears: a return is missing after one of the setError calls.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why are billInput and resultText fields instead of local variables in onCreate?

  • Speed has nothing to do with it here.

  • Right. Only onCreate uses the button, so it can stay local.

  • It works either way; the question is which methods can see the variable afterwards.

Show answer

B. Right. Only onCreate uses the button, so it can stay local.

2You comment out outState.putString(KEY_RESULT, ...), calculate a tip, and rotate. What do you see?

  • The two EditText fields have ids, so they save their own text.

  • The result TextView was set in code, and nothing saved it.

  • The new Activity rebuilds the TextView from XML, and nothing put the old result back.

Show answer

C. The new Activity rebuilds the TextView from XML, and nothing put the old result back.

3Why test TipMath as plain Java before building the screen?

  • It can. Plain Java is just faster to check and has fewer places for a bug to hide.

  • That splits one hard problem (where's the bug?) into two easy ones.

Show answer

B. That splits one hard problem (where's the bug?) into two easy ones.

Key takeaways

  • Prove the logic in plain Java first; then app bugs can only be wiring bugs.
  • Validate every field and return right after setError, so bad input never reaches the math.
  • Views that more than one method needs belong in fields.
  • EditText fields with ids survive rotation on their own; results you set in code need onSaveInstanceState.
  • Break a fix on purpose once, so you know it's really what's doing the work.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Split the bill: add a third field for the number of people and show each person's share.
  • Quick buttons: add 15%, 18%, and 20% buttons that fill in the percent field with setText.
  • Round up: add a button that rounds the total up to the next whole dollar with Math.ceil and works out the tip that makes that happen.

#Further reading

  • Toasts overview (opens in a new tab): durations, and when a Toast is the wrong tool.
  • Handle configuration changes (opens in a new tab): why rotation recreates the Activity and what else triggers it, like switching to dark mode.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what RecyclerView recycles, and why that keeps a 500-item list fast.
  • Build the four pieces of a list: row layout, ViewHolder, Adapter, and LayoutManager.
  • Add RecyclerView 1.4.0 to a project through the version catalog.
  • Create a second Activity and open it with an explicit Intent.
  • Pass values with Intent extras and read them safely on the other screen.

Open your contacts, your messages, or a music app. Same shape every time: a long list you can fling with your thumb, and tapping a row opens a screen about that one thing. That list-then-detail pattern covers a huge share of the apps on your phone. This week you learn both halves.

#Why not just stack 500 TextViews?

You could put 500 TextViews inside a ScrollView. Android would build all 500 before showing the screen, even though about 10 fit on it at once. The app would open slowly and hold hundreds of views in memory that nobody is looking at.

RecyclerView takes a smarter approach. Picture a sushi conveyor belt: the restaurant doesn't own a plate for every piece of sushi it will ever serve. Empty plates come back around, get loaded with something new, and go out again. RecyclerView does that with row views. When a row scrolls off the top, it takes that same view object, fills it with the next item's data, and slides it in at the bottom.

You can watch the idea in a toy model. This is plain Java, not the real RecyclerView: it pretends 10 rows fit on screen and scrolls through 500 songs, counting how many row objects it ever creates.

Position 10 lands in row object #1, the one that held position 0 before it scrolled away. 500 items were shown, but only 10 row objects ever existed. The real RecyclerView keeps a few spare rows ready, so it creates a handful more than that, but the shape is the same: create about a screenful, fill (bind) once for every item shown.

#The four pieces of every list

A RecyclerView never works alone. It always needs these four:

  1. Row layout: an XML file describing one row.
  2. ViewHolder: a small object that holds the views inside one row, so findViewById runs once per row object instead of on every scroll.
  3. Adapter: the bridge between your data (say, a List<String>) and the rows. It creates ViewHolders and fills them.
  4. LayoutManager: decides where rows go. LinearLayoutManager stacks them in a vertical list.

#Add the library

RecyclerView lives in the androidx.recyclerview library. The template's Material library already depends on an older version, so code may compile with nothing added, but you'd be stuck with whatever version Material happens to bring. Add it yourself so you control it. In gradle/libs.versions.toml, add one line to the existing [versions] section and one to the existing [libraries] section (don't create second copies of those headers):

Then in app/build.gradle.kts, inside dependencies { }:

Click Sync Now in the bar that appears at the top of the editor.

#Piece 1: the row layout

Right-click res/layout, choose New > Layout Resource File, and create item_chore.xml:

The row height must be wrap_content. A row with match_parent height fills the whole screen, so you see exactly one item and assume the list is broken.

#Pieces 2 and 3: the Adapter and its ViewHolder

Map the three methods onto the toy model:

  • onCreateViewHolder is new Row(). It inflates a fresh row (turns the XML into real view objects) and wraps it in a ViewHolder. It runs only about a screenful of times.
  • onBindViewHolder is row.text = .... It puts the data for position into a row that already exists, and runs every time a row scrolls into view. Keep it quick.
  • getItemCount tells RecyclerView where the list ends. It never asks for a position past this number.

The false in inflate(..., parent, false) means "use the parent to work out sizes, but don't attach the row yet." RecyclerView attaches rows itself. Pass true and it crashes with IllegalStateException: ViewHolder views must not be attached when created.

#Piece 4: connect it in the Activity

In activity_main.xml:

In MainActivity.onCreate:

You need imports for RecyclerView, LinearLayoutManager, ArrayList, and List; click each red name and press Alt+Enter (Option+Return on a Mac). Run it and the screen shows three rows:

⚠️ Watch out

A blank screen with no crash almost always means setLayoutManager is missing. Logcat says so, if you look: E/RecyclerView: No layout manager attached; skipping layout.

#Changing the list later

The adapter reads from your list, but it doesn't watch it. If you add an item after setAdapter, tell the adapter which position changed, and it animates just that row in:

There are matching notifyItemRemoved(position) and notifyItemChanged(position) methods. Forget to call one, and the screen keeps showing the old list until something else forces a redraw.

#Opening a second screen

In an app built with Views, each screen is usually its own Activity. Create one with File > New > Activity > Empty Views Activity and name it DetailActivity. Android Studio creates three things: the Java file, its layout activity_detail.xml, and an entry in AndroidManifest.xml:

Every Activity must be listed inside <application> in the manifest. Create the class by hand with New > Java Class instead, and the first attempt to open it crashes with android.content.ActivityNotFoundException: Unable to find explicit activity class {...}; have you declared this activity in your AndroidManifest.xml. The exported="false" part means other apps can't open this screen directly, which is what you want for a page inside your own app.

#An explicit Intent names the screen to open

An Intent is a message to Android: "please do this." An explicit Intent names the exact Activity class. You can clip data to it with putExtra, like sticky notes on an envelope:

You never call new DetailActivity() yourself. Android creates it, runs its lifecycle, and keeps your list screen stopped underneath it, ready to come back.

#Reading extras on the other side

In DetailActivity.onCreate:

getStringExtra returns null when the key is missing, so check it. getIntExtra makes you supply a default for the same reason. The keys must match exactly on both sides, and a typo doesn't cause an error; it just gives you null or the default. The fix is to type each key once, as a constant in DetailActivity such as public static final String EXTRA_NAME = "com.example.chores.NAME";, and use the constant on both sides. Starting the key with your package name is the convention Android's docs use.

#Going back

The system Back gesture (or button) finishes DetailActivity and returns to the list, scrolled exactly where you left it, because the list screen was only stopped. To do the same from a button of your own, call finish().

Key takeaways

  • RecyclerView creates about a screenful of rows and rebinds them as you scroll, so long lists stay fast.
  • Every list needs a row layout, a ViewHolder, an Adapter, and a LayoutManager.

  • Tell the adapter when the list changes with notifyItemInserted and friends.
  • An explicit Intent opens a named Activity; extras carry data, keyed by constants so a typo can't break them.

Replace activity_main.xml. A FrameLayout is enough here, since the list is the only thing on the screen:

3 questions

1Why does PlanetAdapter call listener.onPlanetClick(planet) instead of starting DetailActivity itself?

  • The same adapter could then be reused on a screen where a tap does something else entirely.

  • It could, with a Context borrowed from a view. It's a design choice, not a rule.

  • Scrolling speed comes from recycling rows, not from how taps are reported.

Show answer

  • The adapter turns items into rows; it reports taps through an interface and lets the Activity decide what happens.
  • Set everything in onBindViewHolder, including click listeners, because rows get reused.
  • Extra keys are constants on the receiving Activity, shared by both screens.
  • The list screen is stopped, not destroyed, while the detail screen is open, so Back returns to the same scroll position.

What you'll learn

  • Choose where a value should live: a field, a Bundle, a ViewModel, or SharedPreferences.
  • Save and load values with SharedPreferences, and never forget apply().
  • Log messages with Log.d and filter Logcat down to your own app.
  • Read a crash's stack trace and jump to the exact line in your code.
  • Pause a running app at a breakpoint and step through it line by line.
  • Build a debug APK and explain what signing is for.

Type your name into last week's app, swipe the app away from recent apps, and open it again. Your name is gone. The Bundle from two weeks ago only covers rotation and short trips to the background, and a ViewModel doesn't last even that long. Here's the full scorecard:

Where the value lives Rotation Android frees memory in the background Swiped away from recents Phone restarts
A plain field lost lost lost lost
A ViewModel kept lost lost lost
The Bundle (onSaveInstanceState) kept kept lost lost
SharedPreferences kept kept kept kept

Only the bottom row survives everything, because it's the only one written to storage. This week covers the last three things a real app needs: remembering data for good, finding out why something broke, and getting the app onto someone else's phone.

#SharedPreferences: a small saved dictionary

SharedPreferences stores key-value pairs in a private file inside your app's storage. Think of a labeled jar for each value: "username" holds Ana, "high_score" holds 1200. It's the right tool for settings, a high score, a name, or one short note. It is not meant for hundreds of records or for photos; those belong in a database or in files.

#Open the file

Inside an Activity:

"settings" is the file name; use the same name everywhere you read or write. MODE_PRIVATE means only your app can read it, and it's the only mode you should use. Import android.content.SharedPreferences.

#Write, then apply

Changes go through an Editor. Chain the put calls and finish with apply():

apply() updates the in-memory copy right away and writes the file in the background, so the screen never freezes while it saves. There's also commit(), which writes immediately and returns true or false, but it makes the main thread wait for the disk. Use apply() unless you truly need that answer.

The file really is just XML. On an emulator you can usually open it with View > Tool Windows > Device Explorer, under data/data/ followed by your package name and shared_prefs/. After the code above, settings.xml looks like this:

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting apply() is the number one SharedPreferences bug. prefs.edit().putString("username", "Ana"); compiles and runs without a single error, and saves nothing. The Editor collected your change and was thrown away.

#Read, with a default

Every getter takes a key and a default, which is what you get when nothing has been saved yet, like on the very first launch:

The type must match what you saved. Save with putInt and read with getString, and you get a ClassCastException. Keep every key in a constant (private static final String KEY_USERNAME = "username";) so a typo can't quietly create a second, empty key.

A good default pattern: read in onCreate, and write whenever the value changes, or in onPause so nothing is lost if the user leaves suddenly. To wipe saved data while testing, open the phone's Settings > Apps, pick your app, then Storage > Clear storage, or simply uninstall it.

#Logcat: make your app talk to you

System.out.println does work on Android, but the proper tool is android.util.Log, which tags every message and gives it a level:

The letter is the level: v verbose, d debug, i info, w warning, e error. The tag says where the message came from; one constant per class is the usual habit.

Open View > Tool Windows > Logcat while the app runs. Logcat shows messages from the entire phone, often hundreds per second, so you filter it in the search bar:

  • package:mine shows only your app.
  • tag:ScoreKeeper shows only your tag.
  • level:WARN shows warnings and worse.
  • They combine: package:mine level:ERROR.

#Reading a crash

When the app crashes, Logcat prints a stack trace in red. It looks scary, but you only need three lines of it. Here's a typical one (your numbers will differ):

  1. Find the last Caused by: line. That's the real problem: something was null, and the code called setOnClickListener on it.
  2. Just below it, find the first line that names your package (com.example.scorekeeper). MainActivity.java:34 is the exact file and line. In Logcat it's a blue link; click it.
  3. Skip the android.app... lines. That's Android's own code, which called yours.

So the Button on line 34 was null, which means its findViewById id was wrong or belongs to another layout. Three lines read, bug found.

#Breakpoints: freeze the app and look inside

Logs tell you what happened. A debugger lets you stop time and look around while it's happening.

  1. Click in the gutter just to the right of a line number. A red dot appears: that's a breakpoint.
  2. Start the app with Run > Debug 'app' (the bug icon) instead of Run.
  3. When that line is about to run, the app freezes and the Debug window opens.

While it's frozen you can:

  • Read the Variables pane: every local variable and field, with its value right now.
  • Step Over (F8): run this line and stop at the next one.
  • Step Into (F7): go inside the method this line calls.
  • Resume Program: run until the next breakpoint.
  • Right-click the red dot and add a condition like i == 5, so it only stops when that's true.

Reach for a breakpoint when the app doesn't crash but gives the wrong answer. There's no stack trace for a wrong answer. Watching a variable change one line at a time is often the fastest way to see exactly where your logic goes off course.

#Building an APK

An APK (Android Package) is the installable file for an Android app. Every time you press Run, Android Studio builds one and installs it for you. Here's what happens to your files on the way:

To get the file itself, choose Build > Generate App Bundles or APKs > Generate APKs. Older versions of Android Studio call it Build > Build Bundle(s) / APK(s) > Build APK(s); use whichever your menu shows. When it finishes, click locate in the popup. The file is app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk.

#Debug versus release, and why signing exists

Android refuses to install an APK that isn't signed. A signature is like a wax seal on a letter: it proves the file came from whoever holds the key, and that later updates came from the same person. If someone else built a fake "update" to your app, it wouldn't carry your seal, and the phone would refuse it.

  • Debug builds are signed automatically with a debug key Android Studio created for you. They're fine for testing and for sharing with friends.
  • Release builds are optimized and signed with your own key, stored in a password-protected file called a keystore. You make one with Build > Generate Signed App Bundle or APK (older versions: Generate Signed Bundle / APK). The Play Store only takes release builds, uploaded as an app bundle (.aab).

⚠️ Watch out

Back up your keystore and both passwords, and never commit them to GitHub. Anyone with the key can sign apps as you, and if you lose it you can't sign updates to an app you've already shared.

#Installing on a phone

Send the APK to the phone (USB cable, Google Drive, email), tap it, and allow Install unknown apps for whichever app opened it. With the phone plugged in and USB debugging on, adb install app-debug.apk works too.

📝 Note

Google is phasing in developer verification: apps installed on certified Android phones will need to come from verified developers, worldwide starting in 2027. A first phase began on September 30, 2026, for apps from certain stores in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Installing with Android Studio or adb isn't affected. For sharing beyond that, students can use a free limited distribution account that covers up to 20 devices and needs no ID.

4 questions

1A settings screen runs prefs.edit().putString("username", name); when you tap Save. After reopening the app, the name is empty. Why?

  • The Editor collected the change and was thrown away. Add .apply() at the end.

  • Saved preferences survive closing the app and even restarting the phone.

  • You can save from anywhere, including a click listener.

Show answer

A. The Editor collected the change and was thrown away. Add .apply() at the end.

2A crash's stack trace has a dozen at ... lines. Which one do you click first?

  • That's often a wrapper exception from Android's code. The real cause is further down.

  • That's the exact line in your code where things went wrong.

  • The bottom lines are usually deep inside Android's code.

Show answer

B. That's the exact line in your code where things went wrong.

3Your average-score screen shows 50.0 when it should show 80.0, and nothing crashes. What's the most direct way to find the bug?

  • There's no stack trace, because nothing crashed.

  • You'll see exactly which value is skipped or wrong.

  • Building again runs the same wrong code.

Show answer

B. You'll see exactly which value is skipped or wrong.

  • The Bundle survives rotation and background kills, but not being swiped away.

  • It's written to storage, so it survives everything in the scorecard.

Show answer

Key takeaways

  • Only stored data survives the app being swiped away; for small values, that's SharedPreferences.
  • Write with edit(), put..., and apply(). Read with a getter and a default. Keep keys in constants.
  • Log.d(TAG, ...) plus package:mine or tag: in Logcat shows what your app is doing.
  • In a crash, read the last Caused by: and the first line from your own package below it.
  • Breakpoints catch wrong answers that never crash.
  • An APK must be signed: debug builds use Android Studio's key, release builds use your keystore.

Your first job isn't to fix anything; it's to find out which half is broken. Is the note never saved, or is it saved and never loaded? The log lines you added answer that.

Open Logcat and type tag:QuickNote in the search bar. After the run above you'll see three lines like these (the date, time, and process numbers will differ):

Read them like a detective. Saving happens, and 8 characters is exactly Buy milk. Loading happens too, but loading finds nothing. Notice the process number changed from 8123 to 8311: the app really was closed and started fresh. So the bug is somewhere between the save and the load.

#Step 5: Confirm it with a breakpoint

  1. Click the gutter next to the line String saved = prefs.getString("notes", ""); so a red dot appears.
  2. Click Debug 'app' (the bug icon) instead of Run.
  3. The app freezes on that line before it runs. Press Step Over (F8) once.
  4. In the Variables pane, saved is "".

So getString really returns nothing. Now put the two lines side by side: getString("notes", ...) and putString("note", ...). One extra letter. You're reading a key that was never written, and SharedPreferences doesn't complain about that; it just hands back your default.

#Step 6: Fix it for good

You could just delete the s. But the same typo can happen again with any key, so fix the cause: type each key once, as a constant, and use the constant everywhere. Here's the finished MainActivity.java, which also counts saves, wires up the Clear button, and auto-saves whenever you leave the screen:

Two things changed besides the constants. saveNote() reads the old count, adds one, and writes the note and the count in a single edit() chain, so they're saved together. And onPause saves the text every time the screen loses focus, including when you press Home or swipe to recent apps, so a note you forgot to save still survives.

Remove the breakpoint (click the red dot), run normally, type Buy milk, tap Save, swipe the app away, and reopen it. The note is back. The newest Logcat lines, trimmed to the message, read:

The status line says Saved 1 times. That grammar is wrong, and fixing it is the first exercise in this week's practice.

💡 Tip

onPause also runs on rotation, and an EditText with an id keeps its own text across rotation anyway, so the note survives turning the phone too. Try it: type something without saving, rotate, then swipe away and reopen.

#Step 7: Build an APK

  1. Choose Build > Generate App Bundles or APKs > Generate APKs. On older Android Studio versions it's Build > Build Bundle(s) / APK(s) > Build APK(s).
  2. Wait for the popup saying the APK was generated, and click locate.
  3. app-debug.apk is in app/build/outputs/apk/debug/.

Send that file to an Android phone, tap it, and allow installs from that source when Android asks. The Quick Note icon shows up in the app drawer like any other app. Your note won't be on it: each install has its own private storage, so the phone starts with an empty note.

This is a debug APK, signed with Android Studio's automatic debug key. That's fine for friends and testing. A store-ready release needs your own keystore, which this week's practice walks through.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Logcat shows Saved note with 8 characters followed later by Loaded note with 0 characters. What does that tell you?

  • The save line ran, with the right length. Saving isn't the broken half.

  • That's exactly what the breakpoint then confirmed: two different keys.

  • It works the same on emulators and phones.

Show answer

B. That's exactly what the breakpoint then confirmed: two different keys.

2Why replace the string keys with KEY_NOTE and the other constants instead of just deleting the extra s?

  • Speed is the same either way.

  • A misspelled constant name is a compile error, while a misspelled string is silently a different key.

  • Any string works as a key; constants are a safety habit.

Show answer

B. A misspelled constant name is a compile error, while a misspelled string is silently a different key.

3You type a note, don't tap Save, and press Home. Later Android closes the app to free memory. Is the note still there when you reopen it?

  • onPause runs whenever the screen loses focus, before Android ever gets a chance to close the app.

  • The auto-save in onPause covers exactly this case.

  • Rotation has nothing to do with it.

Show answer

A. onPause runs whenever the screen loses focus, before Android ever gets a chance to close the app.

Key takeaways

  • Log both sides of a save-and-load so Logcat can tell you which half is broken.
  • A breakpoint plus the Variables pane turns a guess into a confirmed cause.
  • SharedPreferences returns the default for a missing key, silently, so keep keys in constants.
  • Write related values in one edit() chain, and auto-save in onPause so drafts survive.
  • A debug APK installs on any Android phone, with its own separate storage.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Show when the note was last saved, using System.currentTimeMillis() saved with putLong.
  • Add a character counter under the note that updates as you type, with addTextChangedListener.
  • Ask "Clear this note?" before clearing, using an AlertDialog.

  • Debug your app (opens in a new tab): the full tour of the debugger, including conditional breakpoints and watches.
  • Build and run your app (opens in a new tab): what Run actually does, and how to build for a specific device.

What you'll learn

  • Save and reload text, numbers, and true-or-false settings with SharedPreferences.
  • Read a stack trace and name the exact line in your own code that failed.
  • Use breakpoints to find a bug that gives a wrong answer without crashing.
  • Create a keystore and build a signed release APK.
  • Store a whole list in SharedPreferences by turning it into one string.

These exercises mix new apps with the Quick Note app from the code-along. Anything marked as plain Java runs right on this page, so you can check your logic before moving it into Android Studio. The debugging exercises are about the process: write down what you see at each step, not only the fix.

Warm-up. On a brand-new install, nothing has been saved yet. Predict what each of these returns, then check against the answers in brackets: prefs.getString("name", "") [an empty string], prefs.getInt("high_score", 0) [0], prefs.getBoolean("sound_on", true) [true]. On a first launch, the default is always the answer.

#Exercise 1: "Saved 1 times"

The Quick Note status line says Saved 1 times. Write a method label(int count) that returns these three answers, test it in plain Java, then use it in showSaveCount():

Need a hint?

Three cases means an if, an else if, and an else. Check the special cases (0 and 1) before the general one.

Show solution

In MainActivity, paste label in as a private method (without static) and change showSaveCount() to statusText.setText(label(prefs.getInt(KEY_SAVE_COUNT, 0)));. Android also has plurals resources in XML for exactly this problem; they matter once you translate an app, because other languages have different rules for "1 time" versus "2 times."

#Exercise 2: Welcome back

Make an app with an EditText, a Save name button, and a TextView. The first time it opens, the TextView says Hello, stranger!. After you save Ana, swipe the app away, and reopen it, it says:

Need a hint?

Read the saved name in onCreate with an empty-string default, and pick the greeting based on whether it's empty. Saving happens in the button's listener. Don't forget the last call in the save chain.

Show solution

You'll need imports for SharedPreferences, Toast, and the three widgets. The greeting only changes on the next launch, because it's chosen in onCreate. For an instant update, also call welcomeText.setText(...) inside the listener.

#Exercise 3: Read the crash

A classmate's age app crashes when they tap Check with the box empty. Logcat shows:

Answer three questions: What went wrong? On which line of their code? How would you fix it?

Need a hint?

The exception's name and message are on the third line. For the location, skip every line that starts with java. or android. and look for the first one with their package name.

Show solution
  1. What: NumberFormatException: For input string: "". Integer.parseInt was handed an empty string, which isn't a number.
  2. Where: the first line from their own package, MainActivity.checkAge(MainActivity.java:47). The next line, lambda$onCreate$0 ... :38, is the click listener in onCreate that called checkAge. The java.lang.Integer and android.view.View lines are library code.
  3. Fix: catch the exception and show an error instead of crashing:

The framework line numbers (627, 7659) change with the Android version, which is one more reason to look for your own package name instead.

#Exercise 4: Step through a wrong answer

This program should average three quiz scores. Run it: it prints the wrong value, and nothing crashes.

The right answer is 80.0. Paste average into an Android app (call it from a button and show the result in a TextView). Put a breakpoint on sum += scores[i];, start with Debug 'app', and write down i and sum from the Variables pane each time it stops. Then find the bug.

Need a hint?

Look at the value of i the very first time the breakpoint stops. Which index of the array is that, and which score lives at index 0?

Show solution

At the first stop, i is already 1 and sum is 0. At the second stop, i = 2 and sum = 80. Then the loop ends with sum = 150. The score at index 0 (90) is never added, so the method divides 150 / 3 and gets 50. Arrays start at 0, so the loop must too:

Logcat alone wouldn't have caught this, because nothing crashed and no error was printed. Watching the variables change is what showed that one value was skipped.

#Exercise 5: A setting that sticks

Add a CheckBox labeled "Auto-save when I leave" to Quick Note. Its checked state must be saved the moment it changes, so it's still ticked (or unticked) next launch, and onPause should only auto-save the note when it's ticked.

Need a hint?

A CheckBox has setChecked, isChecked, and setOnCheckedChangeListener. Load the saved value with getBoolean before you attach the listener.

Show solution

In the layout, above the buttons:

Add private static final String KEY_AUTOSAVE = "autosave"; and a field private CheckBox autosaveCheck;, then in onCreate:

And change onPause:

Import android.widget.CheckBox. Calling setChecked before attaching the listener avoids a pointless save at every startup, since the listener would fire for that first setChecked too.

#Exercise 6: A signed release APK

Produce a release APK of Quick Note signed with your own key, install it on a phone, and write down where your keystore lives. This walkthrough shows the wizard you'll use:

Need a hint?

The wizard is under the Build menu, with "Signed" in its name. Save the keystore somewhere outside the project folder, so it can't end up on GitHub by accident.

Show solution
  1. Choose Build > Generate Signed App Bundle or APK (older versions: Generate Signed Bundle / APK), select APK, and click Next.
  2. Under Key store path, click Create new. Choose a location outside your project folder, such as a keys folder in Documents, and name the file quicknote.jks.
  3. Fill in a keystore password, a key Alias (like upload), a key password (Android's docs suggest using the same one as the keystore), and at least your name under Certificate. Leave Validity (years) at 25 or more. Click OK, then Next.
  4. Pick the release build variant and click Create.
  5. When the popup appears, click locate. The file is app/release/app-release.apk.

If the phone already has the debug version, uninstall it first. The two are signed with different keys, so Android refuses to let one replace the other; the phone says the app wasn't installed because it conflicts with an existing package, and adb reports INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE. Newer Android Studio versions may also show a developer verification status for your package name in the wizard; that matters for publishing to the public, not for this exercise.

#Challenge: save a whole list

SharedPreferences only stores simple values, but a to-do list is a List<String>. Write encode(List<String>), which turns the list into one String, and decode(String), which turns it back. Then use them to save and load a list in an app. You may assume no item contains a newline. Your test should print:

Need a hint?

String.join("\n", items) glues a list together with newlines between items, and split("\n") cuts it apart again. Test the empty string separately: what does "".split("\n") give you?

Show solution

The last line shows why the empty-string check exists: "".split("\n") returns one empty item, not zero, so without the check a fresh install would show one blank to-do. In the app, save with prefs.edit().putString("todos", encode(todos)).apply(); and load with decode(prefs.getString("todos", "")). SharedPreferences also has putStringSet, but a Set doesn't keep your list's order and drops duplicates.

What you'll learn

  • List the five things your capstone app must do and the three things you hand in.
  • Pick an idea that fits the requirements and the time you have.
  • Sketch every screen and the moves between them before writing XML.
  • Write and test your model class first, as plain Java.
  • Decide which data is saved for good and which only needs to survive rotation.

For six weeks you've built apps someone else designed: a tip calculator, a planet list, a note that remembers. Now you decide what the app is. The capstone is a chance to make something you'd actually keep on your own phone, and it uses every skill from the course in one project.

#The brief

Build an Android app in Java, with XML layouts, that someone could pick up and use without you explaining it. It must have:

  1. Two or more screens (Activities), with navigation between them using an Intent.
  2. User input: at least one EditText or other control the user fills in, validated so bad input can't crash the app.
  3. State that survives rotation: rotate at any moment and nothing the user sees resets. At least one value must be saved with onSaveInstanceState (or a ViewModel), not only views that save themselves.
  4. A scrolling list built with RecyclerView.
  5. Saved data: close the app completely, reopen it, and the user's data is still there. SharedPreferences is enough.

#What you hand in

  • A project that builds and runs. A fresh copy should open in Android Studio, sync, and run with no errors.
  • A short demo (2 to 3 minutes) in the final class, showing each requirement working, live or as a screen recording.
  • A bug note: a few sentences about one real bug you hit, how you found it (Logcat, a stack trace, a breakpoint), and how you fixed it.

#Picking an idea

The ideas that work best share one shape: a list of things the user creates, plus a screen to add or view one. That shape hits every requirement almost automatically. The list is your RecyclerView, the add screen is your input and your Intent, and the items are your saved data. Here are five ideas at three levels of difficulty:

Idea Level The list shows The second screen What gets saved A stretch feature
Book or movie list Starter Titles with a star rating Add or edit a title, rating, and short review Every title, rating, and review Sort by rating
Flashcards Starter The cards in your deck Quiz mode: tap to flip, mark right or wrong Cards and your best score Shuffle the deck
Habit tracker Standard Habits with current streaks Add a habit, or mark one done today Habits and streaks Reset a streak if a day is missed
Homework planner Standard Assignments by due date Add or edit an assignment The assignment list Highlight anything due tomorrow
Workout log Stretch Past workouts, newest first Log a workout with type and minutes History of every workout Weekly total minutes at the top

You can also invent your own. Test it against the brief with three questions: which screen is the list, what does the user type, and what gets saved? If you can't answer all three in one sentence each, the idea needs another pass.

💡 Tip

Pick something small that you'd really use. A finished, polished habit tracker beats a half-built social network every time, and it makes a much better demo.

#Ideas that cause trouble

  • Anything that needs the internet (weather, chat, logins). Networking wasn't part of this course and can eat your whole schedule.
  • Games with real-time movement. Those need a custom drawing loop, not Views and layouts.
  • Huge amounts of data, like thousands of items or photos. SharedPreferences is built for small amounts.

#Plan before you build

Ten minutes on paper saves hours of rewriting XML. Copy this template into a PLAN.md file in your project's top folder (or onto paper) and fill it in:

#1. What are the screens?

Sketch each screen as a box with its views inside, and draw an arrow for every way to move between screens, labeled with what triggers it. For a habit tracker, the map might be:

Every arrow out of MainActivity will become an Intent, and every arrow back becomes finish() or the Back gesture. If your sketch has an arrow you can't explain that way, sort it out now, while it's only a drawing.

#2. What is one item?

Write the model class first. It forces you to decide exactly what data you're storing, before any screen depends on it. For a habit tracker:

The main method exists only so you can test the class here, before Android is involved. Delete it when you move Habit into your project, and add your package line at the top. Notice that name is final but streak isn't: a habit's name stays fixed after it's created, while its streak changes. Making those choices on purpose is what the model class is for.

#3. What gets saved, and what survives rotation?

Make two short lists:

  • Saved for good (SharedPreferences): the items themselves, plus any settings.
  • Survives rotation (Bundle or ViewModel): whatever the user is in the middle of, like which sort order is selected, a quiz score in progress, or a half-filled form that isn't in an EditText.

If something is on the first list, it's automatically safe through rotation too, as long as you reload it in onCreate or onResume.

#4. What can go wrong with input?

For every field, write what a careless or mischievous user might type: nothing, only spaces, a huge number, letters in a number field, a 500-character name, an emoji. Decide now what the app does in each case. You'll test exactly these cases in the final lesson.

#Schedule

The next lesson walks through each milestone with a starter skeleton you can rename and reshape to fit your idea.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone needs two screens, validated input, rotation-proof state, a RecyclerView, and saved data.
  • "A list of things the user creates, plus a screen to add or view one" fits every requirement.
  • Sketch the screens and arrows first; every arrow becomes an Intent or a Back.
  • Write and test the model class before any layout.
  • List your inputs and their worst cases now, so testing later is a checklist, not a guess.

#Further reading

  • Core app quality guidelines (opens in a new tab): what Android expects from a well-made app, useful as a self-check.
  • Principles of navigation (opens in a new tab): how users expect Back and moving between screens to behave.

What you'll learn

  • Build a large app in small milestones, each ending with something you can run.
  • Adapt a starter skeleton (list screen, add and edit screen, storage) to your own idea.
  • Save a list of objects by encoding it as one string, and test that code as plain Java.
  • Reload the list in onResume so it updates after the second screen closes.
  • Keep a screen setting through rotation with onSaveInstanceState.

Big projects fail in one way more than any other: everything gets written at once, nothing runs, and there are forty red errors with no clue which one matters. The cure is milestones. Each one below ends with a checkpoint, something you run and see working, before you move on. If a checkpoint fails, the bug is in the code you wrote since the last one, which is never very much code.

The skeleton is a generic "entries" app: a list of items that each have a title and a note. Rename it to fit your idea (Entry becomes Habit, Recipe, Workout) and add fields as you go. Here's how its six classes fit together once all five milestones are done:

#Milestone 0: Project setup

Create an Empty Views Activity project (Java, API 24). The code below uses the package com.example.capstone; change every package line to match yours.

Create File > New > Activity > Empty Views Activity named AddEntryActivity. Check that the manifest now has <activity android:name=".AddEntryActivity" android:exported="false" />.

#Milestone 3: Saving and loading

SharedPreferences stores strings, not lists of objects. So saving is split in two: plain-Java code that turns a list of entries into one String and back (easy to test), and a tiny Android class that stores that string.

The format is simple: one entry per line, with the title and note separated by a tab character. Here's the code that does it, inside a test program that runs on this page. The test carries its own copy of Entry at the bottom so it can run alone.

Read the output against the input. The Spanish note had a newline in it, and clean turned it into a space, because a raw newline would have split that entry into two broken lines on reload. The empty Stretch note came back as an empty note instead of vanishing, thanks to the -1 in split("\t", -1), which tells Java to keep empty pieces at the end. It doesn't need to be public, because every class that uses it is in the same package. Don't copy the test's Entry; you already have the real one.

Now AddEntryActivity.java. It adds a new entry, or edits an existing one when it receives an index extra:

Checkpoint: add an entry and tap Save. The screen closes, but the new entry doesn't appear yet, because MainActivity still shows fake data. That's Milestone 4.

#Milestone 4: Connect the list to saved data, plus rotation state

The list has to refresh every time you come back from the add screen. onCreate won't do it, because MainActivity was only stopped while the other screen was open. But onResume runs every time the screen comes back to the front:

Replace MainActivity.java with the full version. It reloads in onResume, passes an index extra for editing, and keeps a sort toggle across rotation with a Bundle:

The sorted copy holds the same Entry objects as allEntries, just in a different order, so indexOf finds each one's real storage index. The sort setting is the capstone's rotation requirement in action: it isn't saved for good (a fresh launch starts unsorted), but it must survive turning the phone.

Checkpoint: add three entries, edit one, swipe the app away and reopen it (all three are still there), switch to A-Z, and rotate (still A-Z).

#Milestone 5: Make it yours

Now turn the skeleton into your app, one change at a time, running after each:

  • Rename Entry and its fields, and add what your idea needs (a number, a date as text, a true-or-false flag). Update EntryCodec to write and read each new field as one more tab-separated piece, and run the plain-Java test again before trying it in the app.
  • Move hard-coded text ("Add entry", "Title") into strings.xml.
  • Add a delete option: a long press, or a Delete button on the edit screen that calls entries.remove(editIndex), then saves and finishes.
  • Show a friendly message when the list is empty, instead of a blank screen.
  • Keep a running bug log in a text file as you go. Your bug note for the demo comes straight out of it.

💡 Tip

Zip a copy of your project folder (or make a Git commit, if you use Git) after every checkpoint that passes. If a later change breaks everything, you can go back to the last version that worked instead of untangling forty errors.
